cc-grp-help.mistakes: Never running /doctor when CLI behaves strangely — it catches 90% of common issues instantly.

pl-cowork.title: Claude Cowork
pl-cowork.what: Agentic task automation built into [[node:pl-desktop|Claude Desktop]] (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise). Claude plans multi-step work, breaks it into subtasks, runs code in an isolated VM on your machine, and writes results directly to your file system. Unlike chat, you describe an outcome — Claude handles every step.
pl-cowork.why: Complex knowledge work — file organization, data analysis, document creation — requires many coordinated steps and local file access. Cowork handles this autonomously so you can step away and come back to finished results.
pl-cowork.when: Organizing a chaotic folder, processing hundreds of receipts, synthesizing research from multiple documents, building spreadsheets with formulas, creating reports. NOT for simple questions — use regular chat instead.
pl-cowork.impact: Hours of repetitive file and document work done while you focus on other things. Can run scheduled tasks automatically (daily, weekly) without any code or APIs.
pl-cowork.example: Task: Sort my Downloads folder by type, extract total amounts from all receipt screenshots, create an Excel report with monthly totals. Claude plans the steps, reads files, runs analysis, and saves the finished spreadsheet — all without your involvement.
pl-cowork.mistakes: Using Cowork for simple Q&A — wastes your usage quota significantly. Closing the Desktop app while a task runs — this stops it immediately. Granting access to your entire drive — connect only the folder you need.

pl-integrations.title: Integrations
pl-integrations.what: Claude connects to external apps and platforms via built-in connectors. Key integrations: Chrome extension (reads/navigates/fills forms in your browser, side panel, tab groups, scheduled browser tasks — paid plans, beta). Microsoft 365 (read-only access to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Word, Excel, PowerPoint — all plans). Google Workspace (Drive, Gmail, Calendar via Plus menu connectors). Slack (search messages, meeting transcripts).
pl-integrations.why: Keeps Claude inside your existing workflow instead of requiring you to copy-paste content between apps. Claude sees the context you're already working in.
pl-integrations.when: Chrome: automating repetitive browser tasks, extracting data from websites, filling forms. M365: asking questions about your emails, documents, meetings without leaving Claude. Google: referencing Drive files or calendar events in chat. Slack: finding past decisions or meeting summaries.
pl-integrations.impact: Eliminates the biggest friction in AI workflows — manually moving context between tools. Claude becomes a layer on top of your existing apps.
pl-integrations.example: Enable M365 connector → ask Claude: 'Summarize the emails from last week about the budget proposal and list open action items.' Claude searches Outlook and Teams, reads the threads, and returns a structured summary.
pl-integrations.mistakes: Expecting M365/Google connectors to take actions (send emails, create docs) — they are READ-ONLY for now. Not granting the necessary permissions when installing Chrome extension — Claude can't see page content without them.

cap-limitations.title: Capabilities & Limitations
cap-limitations.what:
Claude is powerful, but has real limits. Knowing them = not being surprised or frustrated when something doesn't work.

**Key limits:**
- **Knowledge cutoff** — training data ends around early 2026. Claude doesn't know events after that.
- **Hallucinations** — may confidently state false facts, especially on niche topics or while «filling gaps».
- **No real-time data** — without web search enabled, can't see the internet.
- **[[node:b-context|Context window]]** — in long conversations early content «falls out» of memory.
- **No image generation** — text and code only (use Imagen / DALL-E / etc. for drawing).
- **Literal interpretation** — weak at catching sarcasm, cultural nuance, subtext.
cap-limitations.why: Most AI mistakes happen because users don't know the boundaries. Understanding limitations lets you design prompts and workflows that work around them instead of running into them.
cap-limitations.when: Any time you use Claude for factual claims, recent events, long-running tasks, or high-stakes decisions — verify outputs. Never rely solely on Claude for legal, medical, or financial advice.
cap-limitations.impact: Users who understand limitations make 3-5x fewer errors. They verify outputs, use [[node:cap-search|web search]] when needed, break long tasks into shorter sessions, and treat Claude as a first draft rather than a final source.
cap-limitations.example: Bad: 'What is the current stock price of Apple?' — Claude will either refuse or hallucinate. Good: Enable [[node:cap-search|web search]], or ask Claude to reason from what it knows and flag what needs verification.
cap-limitations.mistakes: Treating Claude's confident tone as a signal of accuracy — it is not. Assuming Claude knows recent events — its training has a cutoff. Using one long chat for a multi-day project — context degrades. Not verifying facts on critical documents.

pr-4d.title: 4D Framework
pr-4d.what: Anthropic's meta-framework for effective AI collaboration, co-developed with Ringling College and University College Cork. Four skills that apply to every AI interaction regardless of model or tool: Delegation (choosing what to give AI), Description (writing clear prompts), Discernment (evaluating output critically), Diligence (iterating until the result is safe and accurate). Defines 24 specific behaviors of effective AI use.
pr-4d.why: Most AI failures happen at one of these four stages, not because of the model. A strong prompt to the wrong task (bad Delegation), a correct task with a vague prompt (bad Description), accepting hallucinated output (bad Discernment), or publishing an unverified first draft (bad Diligence). Fixing the stage fixes the failure.
pr-4d.when: Use as a checklist before every significant AI task: Am I delegating the right work? Is my prompt specific enough? Did I verify the output? Is this iteration ready to use? Takes 30 seconds — saves hours of rework.
pr-4d.impact: Users who internalize the 4D Framework produce reliable AI output consistently. It is transferable across all AI tools — skills do not become obsolete when models change.
pr-4d.example: Delegation: 'This research synthesis is suitable for AI.' Description: 'Summarize these 5 articles into 3 key themes for a non-technical audience, max 200 words each.' Discernment: 'Claude cited a statistic I cannot verify — flag it.' Diligence: 'Revise theme 2 — it misses the regulatory angle from article 3.'
pr-4d.mistakes: Skipping Delegation — giving AI tasks that require human judgment (ethical decisions, relationship-sensitive communications). Skipping Discernment — publishing AI output without fact-checking. Stopping at one iteration — Diligence means feedback loops, not a single send.

foundation.title: Claude Foundation
foundation.what:
The base layer: what Claude actually is, how it works, what its limits are. Everything else — [[node:systems|Systems]], [[node:transformation|Transformation]], [[node:use-cases|Use Cases]] — relies on this.

When you read about RAG, multi-agent or workflows in other sections — you'll come back here for context: what model, what [[node:b-context|context window]], what costs.
foundation.why:
Without the Foundation layer the rest is magic. You won't understand why something works one day and not the next, why one model is 15× cheaper than another, why your prompt does fine in chat and breaks in production.

This is the layer where "AI feels like magic" turns into "I know what's going on under the hood".
foundation.when:
Start here if you're new to Claude. Come back here when something stops working in the other layers and you don't understand why.

If you've worked with Claude for 6+ months — you probably know 70% of this. Skim, look for blind spots.
foundation.impact:
After Foundation: you stop being surprised. You know which model to pick for which task. You don't burn through budget on "just to be safe". You don't blame the model when in fact your prompt is the problem.

Main effect: you understand the tool instead of believing in it.
foundation.example:
A typical Foundation question: "Why does Claude give a great answer in chat but trip in the API?"

Answer in Foundation language: in chat you have system prompts from Anthropic + Projects context + conversation history. In the API — you have only what you sent. Same model, different context. Once you get it — you stop being surprised by 80% of "weird" cases.
foundation.mistakes:
Main mistake: skip the basics and dive into "cool stuff" like multi-agent. Six months in you'll be debugging things you don't understand because you skipped the foundation.

Better: spend 2-3 hours on Foundation, then move on. Faster overall than "learn as you go".

systems.title: Systems — how AI works as a system
systems.what:
[[node:foundation|Foundation]] is about "Claude can do X". Systems is about "how to make Claude do X every day, predictably, in a team".

This is the layer where you move from "playing in chat" to "we have a working process". Workflows, data, integrations, monitoring — the things that turn AI from a toy into a tool.
systems.why:
AI in chat is fun, but it doesn't scale. Five people, five different ways to do the same thing. No idea what the team did yesterday. Costs unclear, quality drifting, model changed — what now?

Systems is the answer to all of this. Not "how to write a better prompt", but "how to build something stable".
systems.when:
When you notice:
- AI helps you, but the team uses it however they want — chaos
- You've automated something — now you have no idea if it's still working
- AI costs are growing, no one knows why
- You want to scale your AI experiment from "on the manager's laptop" to "the whole team uses this"
systems.impact:
Without Systems: 80% of AI initiatives die at the pilot stage. "It worked, then quality dropped, no one fixed it."

With Systems: AI features live for years. You see problems in a day, not a month. The team trusts the process — they don't need to check every output manually.

Main point: AI stops being magic and becomes infrastructure.
systems.example:
A typical Systems question: "AI writes email drafts well, but how do we make sure nothing weird ever goes to a client?"

The answer involves several Systems building blocks at once: workflow with steps, quality gate before sending, escalation to a human on edge cases, eval to monitor quality weekly, cost management not to overspend.

That's the difference between "AI helps a manager" and "the team has reliable support powered by AI".
systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: jump into Systems without Foundation. You'll be building workflows without understanding how the model works underneath. You'll be confused why one chain works and another doesn't.

Second mistake: build a System for an unimportant task. Systems take effort. Build them where it matters — frequent, business-critical work. Don't automate something you do once a month.

transformation.title: Transformation — how AI changes the way a team works
transformation.what:
[[node:foundation|Foundation]] = "what Claude can do". [[node:systems|Systems]] = "how to make Claude work like a system". Transformation = "how a team's work changes when AI becomes a real part of it".

This is about changes in your role. Marketer turns from a copywriter into a brand strategist. Designer — from a pixel-pusher into a researcher. Support — from "answering tickets" into "improving the product".
transformation.why:
Tools alone don't change the company. You can buy ChatGPT for everyone and nothing happens — people will keep working the old way.

Real transformation = a change in how teams work, what they measure, what they consider their job. That's the hardest and most valuable part.
transformation.when:
When you sense:
- We have AI tools — but the way we work hasn't really changed
- Each team uses AI on its own — no shared practice
- AI changed individuals — but the team is still organized the same
- Hard to articulate "so what specifically changed in our role"
transformation.impact:
Without Transformation: AI = an individual tool. Everyone uses it differently, no team-wide impact, the leadership can't show what changed.

With Transformation: the team's role visibly shifts in a year. You don't talk about "AI" anymore — you talk about "how we work now". AI is a given, not a feature.

Main point: AI stops being a topic for separate meetings and becomes the new default of how the team works.
transformation.example:
Marketing team before transformation: 3 posts a week, content plans always slipping, brand voice fuzzy, analytics "someday".

A year into transformation: 15 posts a week, brand voice configured in AI (everyone writes consistently), daily analytics in Slack, the team focuses on strategy and creative directions, not on "who's writing what".

The difference isn't "AI tools" — it's a different team that works differently.
transformation.mistakes:
Main mistake: skip Foundation and Systems, jump straight to Transformation. "We're transforming, AI everywhere!" — without solid building blocks underneath the transformation is fake.

Second mistake: top-down transformation. "Everyone now works with AI" in a CEO email = two weeks later everyone is back to the old ways. You need bottom-up traction from teams + top-down support.

Third mistake: measuring transformation in productivity %. Real transformation = a change in what the team considers important and how it spends its time. That's hard to put into a single %.

use-cases.title: Use Cases — ready-made scenarios for your task
use-cases.what:
[[node:foundation|Foundation]] / [[node:systems|Systems]] / [[node:transformation|Transformation]] answer "what / how / why". Use Cases answer "here's exactly what to do for this specific task".

A Use Case is a path: "I need to organize support — read these 5 nodes in this order, watch these 2 tutorials, you'll get a working system in 2 weeks".

It's a shortcut from "there's tons of stuff in the knowledge base" to "here's the path for your situation".
use-cases.why:
The knowledge base has hundreds of nodes. Most people can't and won't read all of it. They want "I need X — show me what to read for that".

Use Cases are pre-assembled answers to the most common "I need X". You don't think about which nodes are relevant — you follow the path.
use-cases.when:
Start with a Use Case when:
- You have a specific business task (organize support, set up brand voice, automate operations)
- You don't know where to start in the knowledge base
- You want to see how nodes connect into a real solution
- You need a result in 2-4 weeks, not "learn AI in general"
use-cases.impact:
Without Use Cases: you spend 2 weeks reading the knowledge base, get tons of theory but no clear answer to "what do I actually do".

With Use Cases: 2 hours through the path → a clear plan → 2 weeks of implementation → measurable result.

Main point: knowledge → action, not knowledge → more knowledge.
use-cases.example:
Use Case "AI in support": you read 5 specific nodes (tier-1 automation, knowledge base, escalation, evals, cost management) + watch 2 tutorials about prompt and Project setup → in 2 weeks you have an AI handling 60% of typical tickets.

If you tried to do this from scratch through the knowledge base — you'd spend a month reading first.
use-cases.mistakes:
Main mistake: think a Use Case will solve everything for you. No — it shows the path. You still have to walk it: read, configure, test on your data.

Second mistake: try to apply someone else's Use Case verbatim to your company. Use Cases are templates. Take 80% from the template, adapt 20% to your specifics.

ai-fundamentals.title: AI Fundamentals
ai-fundamentals.what: Universal AI concepts not tied to any single model: LLM, [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]], vector databases, RAG. The vocabulary every AI system speaks — from ChatGPT to your own pipeline on open-source models.
ai-fundamentals.why: 105 Atlas covers Claude in depth, but the AI industry is broader. To talk with engineers, evaluate vendor proposals, and make architectural decisions — you need the common concepts.
ai-fundamentals.when: When reading a technical doc / proposal with AI terms. When choosing a tech stack. When discussing architecture with your team.
ai-fundamentals.impact: Knowing fundamentals shifts you from «I use AI» to «I understand what I am doing». You gain confidence in decisions and substantive arguments.
ai-fundamentals.example: A RAG pipeline uses [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] (a fundamental concept), stores them in a [[node:af-vector-db|vector database]] (a fundamental technology), and feeds relevant chunks into an LLM (a fundamental architecture). Knowing all three — you can read any RAG documentation.
ai-fundamentals.mistakes: Learning fundamentals as abstract theory. More effective: take a concrete task (e.g., «build search over my docs») and learn the needed concepts as you go.

af-llm-basics.title: What an LLM actually is — plain language
af-llm-basics.what:
You know how iPhone suggests the next word as you type a text? «I'll be...» → phone offers «home / late / there soon». An LLM does the same — predicts the next word based on what came before. Only it wasn't trained on your texts, but on a huge slice of the internet: Wikipedia, books, articles, forums.

Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini — they're all LLMs. Different «models» = different sizes (bigger = smarter, pricier, slower) and different training data.
af-llm-basics.why:
Once you understand AI just **predicts the next word**, all your unrealistic expectations fall away. «Why did AI mess up 47×83?» — because it doesn't calculate, it guesses the next digit. «Why doesn't it remember yesterday?» — because yesterday's conversation isn't in its training data.

It's like understanding that a car isn't a horse. A horse knows the way. A car doesn't. You have to drive it.
af-llm-basics.when:
Before you seriously start using AI at work. Before arguing with a colleague about «AI should / shouldn't do X». Before estimating «how much will this cost» — cost depends on model size.

If you've worked with AI for a year — skip if you want, but check yourself: do you know **why** AI sometimes fails on simple things? If not, come back.
af-llm-basics.impact:
Before: «AI should know, it's AI after all». Surprise when it fails. Endless prompt rewrites.

After: «AI is a smart word-guesser on top of a huge text corpus. Some things it guesses brilliantly, some it gets wrong. I know which is which».

Main point: instead of fighting AI, you start using it correctly.
af-llm-basics.example:
You ask AI: «What's 47 × 83?»

AI guesses: «3901» (correct is 3901 — but AI might miss, e.g. answer «3851»).

Why? It's not a calculator. It's guessing «after 47 × 83 = usually something close to ...». If this exact multiplication wasn't in the training data — you get an approximation.

**Fix:** give AI a calculator as a [[node:cap-tools|tool]] — it'll call it, get the exact answer, then tell you 3901. Not guessing, but real math.
af-llm-basics.mistakes:
Main mistake: thinking AI **knows** facts. It doesn't — it memorized word patterns. Today's news, exact numbers from your report, your colleagues' names — none of that is inside.

Second mistake: trusting AI when it sounds confident. AI always sounds confident — even when making things up (called «hallucination»). Check facts, especially numbers and dates.

af-embeddings.title: Embeddings — how AI understands «by meaning»
af-embeddings.what:
You know how Google Photos finds «all the cats» in your photos, even though you never labeled any? Or how Spotify finds «similar songs» when you play something new?

That runs on **embeddings** — every word, photo, or song gets turned into a set of numbers (a vector). Similar things get similar numbers. AI then just compares: «these two sets of numbers are close → the meanings are close».
af-embeddings.why:
Regular search looks for **exact words**. You type «internet not working» — Google searches pages with the words «internet», «not», «working». If a page is called «WiFi problems at home» — it won't show up, even though it's about the same thing.

Embedding-based search looks **by meaning**. «Internet not working» = «WiFi problems at home» — close number sets → finds both.

It's the same magic that lets AI understand «forgot my password, help» and «how do I reset my password» are the same thing.
af-embeddings.when:
When you need to search large piles of documents and exact-words aren't enough. When you're building search that should «understand» what users mean. When you want recommendations «similar products / docs / customers».

Everything [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] does — stands on embeddings.
af-embeddings.impact:
Before: user asks «email not arriving» → FAQ search returns nothing (FAQ says «email delivery failures») → customer goes to support.

After: embeddings catch «email not arriving» = «email delivery failures» → finds the FAQ → customer self-serves.

Main point: self-service search quality jumps 2-3× without rewriting any content.
af-embeddings.example:
You have a Notion article «Password reset: step-by-step guide». An employee asks the Slack bot: «forgot my password, help».

Without embeddings: bot looks for the word «forgot» in articles. «Forgot» isn't in the title → nothing found → «contact admin».

With embeddings: «forgot my password, help» → number set. «Password reset: guide» → similar number set. Bot finds the article → drops the link → employee solves it in 5 seconds.
af-embeddings.mistakes:
Main mistake: using embeddings from a random model. Old cheap model = bad number sets = bad matches. Solid options today — OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere embed, or natively in Claude.

Second mistake: thinking embeddings = «AI understands meaning like a human». It understands **pattern similarity**. Sometimes finds completely the wrong thing — especially for rare terms or in-house slang.

af-vector-db.title: Vector Database — a library for meanings
af-vector-db.what:
You know how in a library books are shelved by topic, not alphabetically? Pick up a book on gardening — 10 more on gardening sit nearby. Handy when you search by meaning.

A vector database works the same, but for AI. Stores millions of [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] (number sets for meanings) and quickly finds «the 10 closest in meaning to this». Pinecone, pgvector (for Postgres), Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma — these are all vector DBs.
af-vector-db.why:
Without a vector DB embeddings are useless. Imagine you have 50,000 company documents as number sets. When an employee asks a question — you need to find the 5 most relevant in milliseconds.

A regular database (Postgres / MySQL) would take 30 seconds — scanning all 50,000. A vector DB — 50 milliseconds. That's the difference between «works» and «doesn't work in production».
af-vector-db.when:
When you have a [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG system]] with more than 1,000 documents. When you need semantic search across a large knowledge base. When you're building recommendations (similar products / docs / customers).

If you have 50 documents — you don't need one. Keep everything in app memory, process on the fly.
af-vector-db.impact:
Without a vector DB: you try RAG on 50 docs → works → try on 10,000 → every query takes 30 seconds → users leave.

With a vector DB: 1 million documents, 100 millisecond response, thousands of parallel queries. That's the gap between demo and production.
af-vector-db.example:
You have 50,000 knowledge base articles. An employee asks the Slack bot: «How do I file a business trip to Germany?»

What happens:
1. Bot turns the question into an [[node:af-embeddings|embedding]] (number set)
2. Goes to the vector DB: «find 5 articles with the most similar number sets»
3. Vector DB finds in 50 ms: «EU Business Trip Policy», «Visa to Germany», «Expense Filing»
4. Bot hands these 5 to Claude → Claude answers

Result: answer in 2 seconds instead of 30 + manual searching.
af-vector-db.mistakes:
Main mistake: grabbing an expensive managed service (Pinecone, Weaviate Cloud) when pgvector would do. If your team already has Postgres — pgvector adds vector search as an extension. Simple, cheap, under your control.

Managed solutions are needed at > 10 million vectors or with strict latency requirements. Otherwise — you're paying for «fashionable».

af-rag-basics.title: RAG: how AI answers from your documents
af-rag-basics.what:
Remember how at school you opened your cheat-sheet first, and then answered? RAG works the same way. AI gets the question → first pulls relevant chunks from your knowledge base → reads them → forms an answer. Not from its head, but from concrete documents it found.

RAG = Retrieval (found it) + Augmented (added to the prompt) + Generation (wrote the answer). Sounds complex, easy to set up. For the **architecture details** see [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]].
af-rag-basics.why:
AI on its own doesn't know your documents. Ask about your refund policy — it'll either say «I don't know» or invent something plausible (that's hallucination).

With RAG it answers **from your documents** and can cite the source. No invention.

This is the most common way AI is used in companies. Not «AI writes creative copy» — but «AI answers based on our knowledge base».
af-rag-basics.when:
When you have **documents AI needs to know**:
- Support knowledge base
- HR internal policies
- Product documentation
- Customer conversation history
- Archive of meetings and decisions

When AI without RAG says «I don't know» to questions that **do** have answers in your documents — it's time.
af-rag-basics.impact:
Without RAG: AI answers correctly on 30% of questions about your company. The rest — hallucinates or gives up.

With RAG: 80-90% correct answers, with source citations.

Main point: users start **trusting** AI because they see where the answer came from.
af-rag-basics.example:
Customer asks in chat: «What's your return policy for gift cards?»

RAG system:
1. Takes the question → turns it into an [[node:af-embeddings|embedding (number set)]]
2. Searches the document base for «meaning-similar» chunks
3. Finds the section «Returns Policy → Gift Cards: returnable within 30 days, unused»
4. Passes to Claude: «here's the question + here's what we found → answer»
5. Claude: «Gift cards can be returned within 30 days if unused. Source: Returns Policy, section 4.»

Customer gets a precise, sourced answer in 5 seconds.
af-rag-basics.mistakes:
Main mistake: «let's just RAG it and we're done». Naive RAG (found top 3 chunks → handed to AI) works at 50%. Production RAG needs tuning: re-ranking, relevance checks, metadata, splitting documents into the right-sized chunks.

Second mistake: dumping everything into the base — old drafts, duplicates, contradicting versions. AI finds garbage → answers garbage. Cleanliness beats quantity.

af-memory-systems.title: AI memory — why it «forgets»
af-memory-systems.what:
You have 4 types of memory yourself. **What's in the room now** (what you see — short-term). **Notes in Notion** (external — stored long, you search). **Recognizing familiar faces** (semantic — you remember meaning, not details). **Specific events** (episodic — «this was at the March 5 meeting»).

AI has exactly the same 4. When people complain «AI forgot what I said yesterday» — that's not a bug. It means you picked the wrong memory type for the task.
af-memory-systems.why:
Without understanding memory types, you build a chatbot that «doesn't remember» — and don't know what to do. Just expand context window? Expensive and doesn't scale. Plug in a knowledge base? Which one? Each memory type solves its own problem.

It's like with your own memory: you don't try to hold all of Wikipedia in your head. You remember the important things, write down the rest.
af-memory-systems.when:
When designing an AI assistant that needs to **remember** something across conversations:
- Support chatbot that remembers customer history
- AI assistant that remembers your preferences
- Team bot that accumulates decisions and context

If you have one-shot tasks («translate this text») — memory isn't needed.
af-memory-systems.impact:
Without memory architecture: AI = «one-question helper». Starts from scratch every time. User is irritated: «I told you yesterday, did you forget?».

With the right architecture: AI = «colleague who remembers context». Remembers the project, work style, past decisions. Come back a week later — you continue from where you stopped.
af-memory-systems.example:
Chatbot for product managers in SaaS:

- **Short-term (in-context):** in this conversation remembers «you're currently discussing feature X»
- **External (RAG):** [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] connected to spec base and customer interviews
- **Semantic (Memory tool):** remembers «this PM works on a B2B product, prefers data-driven approach»
- **Episodic (history log):** stores specific decisions «April 3: decided to launch feature X in beta»

When PM asks «what did we decide about feature X?» — AI goes to episodic → finds the decision → answers with the date.

More in Claude: [[node:cap-memory|Memory tool]], [[node:p-files|Project Files]], [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]].
af-memory-systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: «let's just expand the context window to a million and AI will remember everything». Expensive, slow, doesn't work in production. AI gets lost when context is too big («lost in the middle»).

Second mistake: cramming everything into one memory type. Current conversation in a RAG base — pointless, fills it with garbage. Long customer profile in every request context — overpay. Each type for its own job.

af-multimodal.title: Multimodal AI — AI that sees and hears
af-multimodal.what:
AI used to only work with text: «write an email», «translate this article». Multimodal AI handles different data types at once: text + images + audio + video.

You can show AI a screenshot of an error and ask «what's wrong here?». Or photograph an invoice and ask «put these numbers into Excel». Claude sees and reads the image, understands what's there, answers.
af-multimodal.why:
The real world isn't text. A designer shows a mockup, a marketer posts an infographic, an accountant scans a receipt. If AI only understands text — it only covers half the tasks.

Multimodal AI opens up tasks that used to require a human or specialized software: receipt reading, chart analysis, mockup understanding.
af-multimodal.when:
When the task needs more than text:
- Screenshot with error → «why isn't this working?»
- Design mockup → «build the HTML»
- Receipt photo → «extract amount and date»
- Chart from a report → «describe the trend»
- Meeting video → «short summary»

If your task is mostly text — multimodal isn't needed.
af-multimodal.impact:
Before: parsing trip receipts — a secretary spends 30 minutes typing amounts into Excel.

After: you send AI 10 receipt photos → AI extracts dates and amounts → 2 minutes for you to review.

Main point: tasks that needed «human eyes» are now done by AI.
af-multimodal.example:
Situation: someone sent you a screenshot with a Python error — a long stack trace, unclear where the problem is.

Before: you re-type the error text into AI chat (10 minutes of fiddling), then ask.

With multimodal: drop the screenshot in → «what's wrong?» → Claude sees the whole stack trace, finds the specific line: «on line 47 your `data` variable is None, but you're trying to access its attribute. Add an `if data is not None` check».

Screenshot to answer — 10 seconds.
af-multimodal.mistakes:
Main mistake: thinking multimodal = «AI sees everything like a human». Reality:
- Recognize objects in photos — good
- Read printed text — good
- Read handwriting — worse than specialized OCR
- Understand a busy chart with many lines — may err
- Count objects precisely in a photo — weaker

Test on your task types — don't trust generic promises.

af-fine-tuning.title: Fine-tuning vs Prompting — train or explain
af-fine-tuning.what:
Imagine you're hiring a new employee. Two options:

1. **Prompting** = give them instructions each time. «Today do it this way, tomorrow that way». Fast, flexible, you can change the approach in a minute.

2. **Fine-tuning** = «train» them for 6 months so they just know without reminders. Expensive, slow, but then works without explanation.

For 95% of tasks **prompting + examples** ([[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot]]) is enough. Fine-tuning is a last resort.
af-fine-tuning.why:
Fine-tuning sounds cool («our own AI!»), but it's tech debt. In 3 months a new Claude version drops — better than your fine-tuned one. To use it — you fine-tune again. A quarter has passed, $10k spent, and you're still on the old model.

Prompting is instant. Change the text in the prompt — AI behavior changes. Want a new model — just switch, everything works.
af-fine-tuning.when:
Fine-tuning makes sense when:
- **Distinct style / tone** that doesn't transfer via prompt examples (rare)
- **Narrow domain** where you have THOUSANDS of input-output pairs (medicine, law)
- **You need cheaper and faster** — fine-tune a small model to replace a big one

In all other cases — prompting + RAG + tools. If you haven't tried that — don't even think about fine-tuning yet.
af-fine-tuning.impact:
The right choice saves months. Teams hear «fine-tuning» → decide it's magic → spend a quarter gathering training data → ship, it works at 80%.

At the same time another team wrote a 10-line prompt + plugged in [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] → they shipped at 85% in a week.

Main point: don't confuse «fashionable» with «needed».
af-fine-tuning.example:
Task: «AI answers customers in our CEO's voice — concise, friendly, no jargon».

**Try prompting first:**
```
System: Reply like our CEO. Style: concise, friendly, no corporate jargon.

Example 1: Q «when will feature X ship?» — CEO would say: «Soon. Next week. Thanks for waiting.»
Example 2: Q «why is it expensive?» — CEO would say: «Because we pay people well. It's worth it.»
[3-5 more examples]
```

50 prompt iterations → if it still doesn't sound like the CEO → then think fine-tuning. 80% of cases — the prompt is enough.
af-fine-tuning.mistakes:
Main mistake: fine-tuning «just in case» from day one. Like tuning a car you haven't driven yet. Learn to drive first.

Second mistake: thinking fine-tuning = «AI gets smarter». No — it gets «more like your data», but may answer WORSE on questions outside that data. It's specialization, not an upgrade.

ai-native-operations.title: AI for operations teams
ai-native-operations.what:
Operations are the people who keep the company afloat: HR, finance, legal, procurement, IT. Tons of repetitive tasks: approve a vacation, categorize an invoice, update a policy, answer a routine question.

AI here doesn't make a "revolution" — it removes the routine. Frees up 2-3 hours a day per person to do what they couldn't get to before.
ai-native-operations.why:
Operations is the most "invisible" work in a company. When it works — nobody notices. When it breaks — panic. AI helps it work predictably and without heroics.

It's not about "replacing people". It's about "your team of 5 no longer has bottlenecks".
ai-native-operations.when:
When you notice:
- One person = one bottleneck ("without Mary nothing gets processed")
- Tons of routine requests distract from important work
- Policies exist but nobody remembers them — everyone asks each other
- Monday reports = 3 hours of copying into Excel
- New hires spend 2 weeks figuring out where things are
ai-native-operations.impact:
Before: HR spends 60% of time on routine questions about vacations / sick leave / certificates. After: AI answers 70% of these itself, HR works on onboarding, development, culture.

Before: finance takes 2 days for a monthly report. After: AI assembles a draft in an hour, finance spends 4 hours reviewing and analyzing.

Main point: operations people stop being "request handlers" and become strategists.
ai-native-operations.example:
5 directions inside:
- [[node:ops-process-automation|Process automation]]
- [[node:ops-decision-intelligence|Decision support via AI]]
- [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Regular reporting]]
- [[node:ops-resource-optimization|Resource optimization]]
- [[node:ops-team-workflow|Team workflows]]
ai-native-operations.mistakes:
Main mistake: try to automate everything at once. "Full AI operations transformation" — sounds great, in practice nobody uses it.

Better: pick one pain (e.g. routine HR questions) → close it with AI → see a result in 2 weeks → move to the next.

Second mistake: automating without the team's involvement. If HR didn't help configure it — they'll sabotage it. AI should be a tool operations people want to use.

ops-process-automation.title: AI Process Automation
ops-process-automation.what: Automating recurring processes via AI: input (trigger) → AI processing → output (result + next action). Skills + Hooks + RAG as the core stack.
ops-process-automation.why: Every team has 30-50% of tasks = recurring: onboarding, status updates, routine comms. AI handles most of these without quality loss.
ops-process-automation.when: When a task happens ≥5×/week + has clear inputs/outputs + result can be validated. Ideal candidates: weekly reports, customer welcome emails, internal status digests.
ops-process-automation.impact: Time savings: 70-90% on a specific task. Consistency: a single quality result instead of «depends who did it».
ops-process-automation.example:
Workflow «Weekly status digest»:
1. Trigger (Monday 9am or /command).
2. AI Step: reads Linear/Jira for the week.
3. AI Step: writes executive summary in branded style.
4. Quality gate: human does final review (15 min instead of 2 hours of writing).
5. Output: publish in #leadership Slack.

Before: 2h/week. After: 15min review.
ops-process-automation.mistakes: Automating a process that has not yet «stabilized». If the process changes every week — AI automation will constantly break. First: stabilize the process manually. Then: automate.

ops-decision-intelligence.title: AI Decision Intelligence
ops-decision-intelligence.what: AI as a «second opinion» for operational decisions: AI analyzes data + context + history of decisions → gives a structured recommendation. Does not replace human, but disciplines the process.
ops-decision-intelligence.why: Operational decisions are often made «by gut» under pressure. AI structuring forces consideration of alternatives, risks, metrics — reduces reactive decisions.
ops-decision-intelligence.when: Hire/no-hire decisions. Resource allocation. Vendor selection. Process change vs no-change. Decisions with >$10k impact or >2 weeks horizon.
ops-decision-intelligence.impact: Reduction in reactive decisions: 50-70%. Decision quality measurable (track outcomes).
ops-decision-intelligence.example:
Decision template:
1. Context: situation in 5 sentences.
2. Options: 3 decision variants.
3. Each option: pros, cons, cost, risk.
4. AI analysis: pattern-matching with past decisions + recommendation.
5. Human override + log decision reasoning.

After 3 months you SEE the patterns of your decisions — where AI was right, where it erred.
ops-decision-intelligence.mistakes: Blindly following AI recommendation. AI is good at pattern analysis but does not know your full context. Treat AI as a «thoughtful junior»: gives perspective, but the decision and accountability are yours.

ops-reporting-automation.title: AI Reporting Automation
ops-reporting-automation.what: Auto-generating reports from structured data: CRM, analytics, project management. AI reads data, writes insight-driven narrative, forms action items.
ops-reporting-automation.why: Teams spend 4-8 hours a week on manual reporting. AI handles 80% of the work, leaving the human with review and executive judgment.
ops-reporting-automation.when: Regular reports (weekly/monthly). Data in systems with API/export. Audience expects consistency in format. KPIs are countable.
ops-reporting-automation.impact: Time-to-report: 4 hours → 30 minutes. Before: different people, different templates. Now: one format, one tone, everywhere. Reports arrive on time, not «when I got around to it».
ops-reporting-automation.example:
Sales Weekly Report:
1. Export from CRM (HubSpot/Salesforce) → CSV.
2. Project with [[node:b-system|system prompt]]: «you are a sales analyst, report format is XYZ».
3. Prompt: «here is data for the week, write executive summary + 3 action items».
4. Output: ready report with numbers, trends, recommendations.

Metrics: reporting time 4h→30min, data accuracy 100% (autopull), insights consistency 95%.
ops-reporting-automation.mistakes: Doing «AI generates pretty text» without action. A report without action items is trash. Structure must be: what changed → why → what we do → KPI. Every time.

ops-resource-optimization.title: AI Resource Optimization
ops-resource-optimization.what: AI optimization of team resource allocation: capacity planning, tools for different tasks, Claude model choice (Haiku vs Sonnet vs Opus), API cost management.
ops-resource-optimization.why: Operations teams often overspend on tools and resources because «we have always done it this way». AI audit reveals over-provisioning, model mismatch, idle resources.
ops-resource-optimization.when: Quarterly resource review. Before annual budget planning. When AI spend becomes visible in P&L.
ops-resource-optimization.impact: Cost reduction: 20-40% on operations spend. Productivity: better tool-to-task fit.
ops-resource-optimization.example:
AI Spend Audit:
1. Export all AI-API logs for 30 days.
2. AI analysis: «which tasks use Opus, can they be moved to Sonnet?»
3. Output: list of tasks + alternative models + estimated savings.
4. Test: one week on the new mix → measure quality.
5. Roll out: if quality does not drop, move 80% of tasks.

Real case: $5k/month Opus → $1.2k/month Sonnet, quality drop <5%, ROI = 4x.
ops-resource-optimization.mistakes: Optimizing only cost without quality measurement. A cheaper model can «save» $1000 but reduce conversion by $5000. Track quality metrics in parallel with cost.

ops-team-workflow.title: AI Operations Team Workflow
ops-team-workflow.what: How an ops team orchestrates working with AI: shared prompts, shared Projects, access, knowledge management. This is about team operating model, not individual usage.
ops-team-workflow.why: Individual AI usage does not scale. A team of 10, each with their own prompting style = different results + duplicated work. Team workflow creates a unified standard.
ops-team-workflow.when: When the team ≥3 people actively use AI. When inconsistent results emerge. When a newcomer arrives and «does not know how we work with AI».
ops-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: a team of 5 does what used to take 8. New hire onboarding: 2 days instead of 2 weeks. Knowledge isn't locked «in Mary's head» — it lives in shared Projects + [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]].
ops-team-workflow.example:
Operations Team Setup:
1. Shared Claude Project «Operations Workspace» with team-style [[node:b-system|system prompt]].
2. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] in shared repo: rules, templates, typical tasks.
3. Reusable Skills for recurring tasks (report-writer, decision-analyzer).
4. Weekly «AI office hours»: team shares discoveries.
5. Metric: % of tasks done through shared workflow.

Stage 3 sign: a newcomer is productive in 2-3 days, not weeks.
ops-team-workflow.mistakes: Making «team workflow» = «one person forces everyone to use their prompts». That is not workflow, that is dictatorship. Team workflow = collaborative development + ownership + feedback loops.

uc-ai-reporting-launch.title: Launch AI Reporting
uc-ai-reporting-launch.what: Full path from «we have manual reports» to «working weekly report workflow». Path through 6 105 Atlas nodes: Foundation → [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI Fundamentals]] → Configuration → Transformation.
uc-ai-reporting-launch.why: This is the most common ops-team request: «AI can write reports, how do we start?». A Use Case gives a clear route instead of «start reading everything».
uc-ai-reporting-launch.when: When there is a regular report (weekly/monthly) taking ≥3 hours per week. When data is available (CRM/analytics with export). When there is team buy-in.
uc-ai-reporting-launch.impact: Outcome: working weekly report workflow in 2 weeks of work. Metrics: time-to-report 4h→30min, consistency +90%, team buy-in measurable (NPS survey).
uc-ai-reporting-launch.example:
Path (6 steps through nodes):
1. Foundation: prompting → how to write a [[node:b-system|system prompt]] for a report
2. Foundation: af-rag-basics → if the report needs CRM context, how to feed it to Claude
3. Foundation: projects → create a «Weekly Reports» workspace for the team
4. Foundation: i-claudemd → describe the report format in [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]
5. Transformation: ops-reporting-automation → concrete workflow with stages
6. Transformation: sc-data → how to work with CSV data

Day 1-3: Setup Project + write first prompt manually.
Day 4-7: Iterate on 5-10 real reports.
Day 8-14: Roll-out to the team + feedback.

Stage transition: 1→2.
uc-ai-reporting-launch.mistakes: Wanting «full automation» in the first week. First AI writes a draft → human edits → measure quality. Only after 5-10 successful iterations — add automation (triggers, scheduling).

uc-ai-process-automation.title: Automate a Recurring Process
uc-ai-process-automation.what: Path to automating a specific operations process via AI. From candidate identification to a production-ready workflow with Skills + Hooks.
uc-ai-process-automation.why: Operations teams often get stuck at «we tried Claude, liked it» — but do not know how to make it systematic. This UC shows a structured approach.
uc-ai-process-automation.when: When there is a process running ≥5×/week with clear inputs/outputs. When result variability is a problem. When there is technical capability for triggers/integrations.
uc-ai-process-automation.impact: Outcome: automated workflow with quality gates in 2-3 weeks. Metrics: time savings 70-90%, error rate <5%, team satisfaction +.
uc-ai-process-automation.example:
Path (6 steps):
1. Identification: pick the process — this is ops-process-automation
2. Foundation: skills + s-create → build a reusable Skill
3. Foundation: mcp → if external integrations are needed
4. Foundation: cc-hooks → automatic triggers
5. Foundation: prompting → core workflow prompt
6. Transformation: ops-process-automation → structure with quality gates

Week 1: Document the process as-is. Identify AI-replaceable steps.
Week 2: Build the Skill + first tests on historical data.
Week 3: Production roll-out with monitoring.

Stage transition: 1→2 (if first automation) or 2→3 (expansion).
uc-ai-process-automation.mistakes: Automating without stabilizing the process. If the process is still changing — the workflow will constantly break. And: not making quality gates. Without human review = automated trash.

uc-ai-decision-support.title: AI Support for Operational Decisions
uc-ai-decision-support.what: Rolling out AI structuring for operational decisions in the team. From ad-hoc «let us discuss in Slack» to a structured decision process with AI analysis.
uc-ai-decision-support.why: Operations teams make 5-10 decisions a week under load. Without structure — lots of reactive, little learning. AI adds discipline without bureaucracy.
uc-ai-decision-support.when: When decisions require trade-off analysis (hire vs no-hire, vendor selection, process change). When retrospective shows «we decided this a year ago and forgot».
uc-ai-decision-support.impact: Outcome: working decision process with AI support in 3-4 weeks. Metrics: reactive decisions ↓50-70%, learning loop established (retrospective with AI pattern matching).
uc-ai-decision-support.example:
Path (6 steps):
1. Identification: which decisions to include (Operations: hires, vendors, processes)
2. Foundation: prompting + pr-cot (chain-of-thought) — structure of AI analysis
3. Foundation: sc-data + sc-analysis — how to feed data for the decision
4. Foundation: af-llm-basics — understand AI boundaries: where it gives value, where it errs
5. Foundation: projects → «Decision Log» workspace with history
6. Transformation: ops-decision-intelligence → concrete workflow

Week 1: Pilot on 3-5 simple decisions.
Week 2-3: Refine template + verify quality.
Week 4: Roll-out to all major decisions + retrospective.

Stage transition: 2→3.
uc-ai-decision-support.mistakes: Using AI as «the decider». AI is good at structuring and pattern matching, but context and accountability belong to the human. Documentation matters more than the AI output itself: track outcomes → learn → improve.

ai-workflows.title: AI Workflows — how AI gets the task done step by step
ai-workflows.what:
A workflow is when you drop a file → AI parses it → you get a summary. Or: an incoming email → AI classifies → drafts a reply → you tweak → send. A workflow is a sequence of steps where AI does its part and you do yours.

Every AI tool you already use (Notion AI, Gmail Smart Reply, meeting transcribers) is a workflow. Someone just hid it behind a button.
ai-workflows.why:
When you do the same thing manually 5 times a week — that's a signal you need a workflow. Configure AI once → it works on its own from then on. You move from "open chat → copy → paste" to "press a button → get a result".

This is the difference between "playing with ChatGPT" and "I have an AI assistant that does X for me".
ai-workflows.when:
When you notice:
- You do the same action more than 3 times a week
- You copy text from one place to another
- AI helps, but every time you have to re-explain
- A team of 3+ does the same task — everyone in their own way
ai-workflows.impact:
Before: sorting email — 1 hour each morning. After: AI sorted it overnight → you spend 10 minutes in the morning checking.

Before: writing a meeting recap — 40 minutes. After: AI pulled decisions and action items from the recording → you tweak for 10 minutes.

Main point: you don't "do it faster", you "do only the important part".
ai-workflows.example:
Workflow "handle an incoming customer email" (for the pattern itself see [[node:sys-workflows-basics|What an AI Workflow really is]] and [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]]):
1. Email arrives at support@
2. AI reads and categorizes: question / complaint / cancellation
3. If a question → AI drafts a reply based on the knowledge base
4. If a complaint → AI calls a human with a ready-made summary
5. You glance at the draft → tweak 1-2 words → send

Result: 50 emails per day instead of 15. Not because you type faster — because AI removed "start from scratch".
ai-workflows.mistakes:
Main mistake: trying to build a workflow "that does everything". Better 5 simple workflows for specific tasks than one giant one.

Second mistake: automating everything. If a step requires human judgement (important client, legal risk, money) — leave it to a human. Workflow ≠ autopilot.

sys-workflows-basics.title: What an AI Workflow really is — in plain terms
sys-workflows-basics.what:
A workflow is a chain of steps: something comes in → AI processes it → result is checked → passed on. For example: email arrives → AI reads → classifies type → drafts reply → human reviews → sent.

This is NOT a single chat prompt. And NOT just "trigger-based automation". The simplest form — [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]] (A → B → C). A workflow is when you have "input → AI → output" that works the same way every day.
sys-workflows-basics.why:
When you work with AI in chat — you re-explain context every time. That's fine for a one-off. But if you do the same thing 50 times a week — you need a workflow: configure once → it repeats.

A workflow turns "AI helps me" into "I have a process, AI is part of it".
sys-workflows-basics.when:
When the task repeats more than 3 times a week.

When you notice:
- "I'm writing this same prompt again"
- "I'm copying data back and forth again"
- 5 people on the team do the same thing — each in their own way
- Quality depends on mood and tiredness
sys-workflows-basics.impact:
Before: every morning 1 hour sorting email. After: AI sorted it overnight, you spend 10 minutes checking.

Main point isn't "faster", it's "predictable". Workflow gives stable quality: 9 out of 10 times the result is good, you know what to expect.
sys-workflows-basics.example:
Workflow "prepare for a customer meeting":
1. In the morning AI checks your calendar
2. For each meeting it finds the customer profile in the CRM
3. Pulls the latest email thread
4. Writes a brief summary: "yesterday discussed X, open items Y, pain points Z"
5. By 8:00 your Slack has summaries for all meetings of the day

You walk into the meeting prepared, not "hold on, let me remember".
sys-workflows-basics.mistakes:
Main mistake: try to build a "universal workflow for everything". You'll end up with a monster nobody understands.

Better: 5 simple workflows for specific tasks. Each does one thing well.

Second mistake: automating a step that requires human judgement. If AI decides "should I send this to the client" — sooner or later it'll send something inappropriate.

sys-linear-chain.title: Linear Chain — a simple sequence of steps
sys-linear-chain.what:
The simplest kind of workflow: A → B → C. Each step takes the output of the previous one. No branches, no "if-then". Just a straight line.

Sounds primitive, but 80% of real AI tasks look exactly like this. No need to overcomplicate upfront.
sys-linear-chain.why:
A simple chain is easy to fix. If something goes wrong — you can see at which step it broke. You add complex branching only when you really can't do without it.

Rule: start with a linear chain. If it covers 80% of cases — leave it. Add complexity when you hit a wall.
sys-linear-chain.when:
When the task splits into clear sequential steps. One step — one meaning.

Examples:
- Transcribe audio → extract decisions → send to Notion
- Receive an article → translate → check terminology → publish
- Read a resume → extract skills → match to job → score
sys-linear-chain.impact:
Linear chain works 9 times out of 10. When it breaks — you can tell where (you see which step failed).

Complex branching workflows work 6 times out of 10, and it's unclear what to fix.

Simplicity = reliability.
sys-linear-chain.example:
Workflow "onboard a new customer":
1. Manager fills out a form with basic customer info
2. AI generates a personalized welcome email
3. AI creates an onboarding checklist tailored to their industry
4. AI drafts a contract with the right pricing
5. Manager checks everything → sends

Each step is simple. If AI got step 3 wrong — manager sees "wrong industry in checklist" → fixes it → moves on. To stop errors reaching the client — put a [[node:sys-quality-gates|Quality Gate]] before sending. No need to redo everything.
sys-linear-chain.mistakes:
Main mistake: add branching from the start ("if enterprise, ..., if SMB, ..."). Result: a workflow nobody understands, impossible to maintain.

Better: build 2 separate linear chains — one for enterprise, one for SMB. Simpler and clearer.

Second mistake: bundling 3 actions into one step ("read the document, summarize, translate to English"). Split them — debugging is 10× easier.

sys-quality-gates.title: Quality Gates — check before passing it on
sys-quality-gates.what:
A point between workflow steps where the result is checked before going further. Either AI checks it (by rules), or a human does.

Without checks, errors pile up. AI got step 1 wrong → step 2 gets garbage → step 3 confidently sends nonsense to a client. (Related: [[node:sys-escalation-paths|escalation to a human]] when a gate fails.)
sys-quality-gates.why:
AI gets things wrong 5-15% of the time. That's fine. What's not fine — letting errors slip down the chain.

A gate catches mistakes early, when they're cheap. Fix at step 2 = 1 minute. Explaining to a client later = a week of damage.
sys-quality-gates.when:
Anywhere an error is costly:
- Before sending to a client
- Before writing to a database
- Before charging money
- Before publishing on social media
- Before passing to a lawyer

Where "we can redo it" — gates aren't needed.
sys-quality-gates.impact:
Without gates: 1 in 10 results goes to a client with an error. Once a month — a major incident.

With gates: 1 in 100 errors slip through. No major incidents — caught either by AI rule-check or by a human.

Main point: you can relax about running AI on real tasks.
sys-quality-gates.example:
Workflow "send a contract to a customer":
1. AI generates the contract from template + customer data
2. **Gate 1 (AI):** check that all required fields are filled, amounts match the CRM, no duplicate paragraphs
3. If the gate failed → return to step 1 with a note on what to fix
4. **Gate 2 (human):** lawyer scans for 30 seconds → ok / not ok
5. If both gates pass → send

Result: 95% of contracts go without lawyer involvement. The lawyer only spends time on edge cases. Zero number errors.
sys-quality-gates.mistakes:
Main mistake: a gate at every step. The workflow becomes "AI works 10 seconds → human reviews 5 minutes → AI works 10 seconds → human reviews...". Nobody will stand it.

Better: gate only before actions with consequences (send, write, charge).

Second mistake: "AI checks AI" as a gate. If the main model made a mistake — the checking model will make the same one. You need either a different check principle (rules, not AI) or a human.

ai-data-systems.title: AI Data Systems — how AI works with YOUR documents
ai-data-systems.what:
You know how Google searches websites and finds the right one? AI Data Systems is the same search, but over YOUR documents: team PDFs, Notion notes, Slack threads, CRM customer records.

Without this AI only knows what was in the internet at training time. With this — AI knows what your team knows.
ai-data-systems.why:
Without data systems AI says "I don't know" to any company-specific question. With data systems — it says "here's the doc from March 14th, it says X, here's the link".

That's the difference between "AI as Wikipedia" and "AI as a new hire who has read the entire knowledge base".
ai-data-systems.when:
When you notice:
- You ask AI about your company — it gives generic answers
- The team has a "person who remembers where things live" — a bottleneck
- New hires spend 2 weeks finding the right documents
- Customers ask the same questions — the answers exist, but they're scattered
ai-data-systems.impact:
Before: "where's our refund process?" → 30 minutes searching Notion + Slack. After: ask AI → link to doc + quote in 5 seconds.

Before: a new hire asks 20 questions in week one. After: they ask AI, only go to colleagues with genuinely complex things.

Main point: the company's knowledge stops being "in Mary's head".
ai-data-systems.example:
We connect AI to a Notion base with company policies (under the hood — [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]). An employee asks in Slack: "How do I file a 5-day business trip to Berlin?"

AI:
1. Searches Notion for relevant documents (regulations, expense policy)
2. Finds 3 documents
3. Assembles the answer: "Per the 2024-03 policy (link): book flights through Concur, hotel up to €180/night, expenses within 5 days via Bookkeeper. Business trips to Germany require 7-day notice to HR."
4. Employee gets the answer in 10 seconds instead of an hour of searching
ai-data-systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: hook up "all documents" at once. You get noise — AI answers citing a 2019 draft.

Better: connect 1 source (current policies) → check answer quality → then add the rest.

Second mistake: not showing sources. If AI answers without a link to "where it got it" — nobody trusts it.

sys-rag-architecture.title: RAG — how AI fetches the right document from your base
sys-rag-architecture.what:
You know how Google searches websites? RAG is the same search, but over your documents, plus an AI that assembles an answer from what it found.

The word RAG sounds scary, but the idea is simple: 1) user asks, 2) the system finds 3-5 relevant chunks from the base, 3) AI composes an answer with citations.
sys-rag-architecture.why:
Without RAG, AI can only do what it learned in training. Ask about your company — it gives generic answers or makes things up.

With RAG — AI answers "here's the doc from March 14th, here's what it says, here's the link". Stops making things up, starts citing.
sys-rag-architecture.when:
When AI should answer based on your documents:
- Company knowledge base
- Internal policies
- Product documentation
- Customer conversation history
- Any data not on the public internet (see [[node:ai-data-systems|AI Data Systems]] for the big picture)

If AI can answer from general knowledge — RAG isn't needed.
sys-rag-architecture.impact:
Simple RAG (fetch — feed to AI): works well on 50-60% of queries.

RAG with relevance checks on what's found: 75-85%.

RAG with clarifying questions and re-ranking: 90%+.

Main point: users stop getting "sorry, I don't know" on questions whose answers are in the docs.
sys-rag-architecture.example:
SaaS product support:
1. Customer writes: "how do I export a report with a region filter for the quarter?"
2. RAG searches product docs — finds 3 relevant sections
3. AI assembles the answer: "Go to Reports → Export. Pick the Region filter, period Custom → set the quarter. Details: link to docs. If Region filter is disabled — you're on Starter plan, upgrade here."
4. Customer gets a concrete answer with links in 5 seconds instead of waiting for an agent

Self-service conversion: from 20% to 70%.
sys-rag-architecture.mistakes:
Main mistake: dumping everything into the base — old drafts, duplicates, outdated policies. AI finds noise and confidently cites a 2019 doc.

Better: fewer documents, but current ones. Set up a process for removing the outdated.

Second mistake: not showing sources. If AI answers without a link to "where it got it" — nobody trusts it, everyone goes to a human anyway.

sys-context-passing.title: How to pass context between steps
sys-context-passing.what:
In a multi-step workflow (see [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]] and [[node:sys-workflows-basics|workflow basics]]) there's a question: what exactly do you pass to the next AI step? Everything that came before? Only the important part? A compressed summary?

Three options:
1. **Pass everything** — simple, but expensive and slow
2. **Pass only what's needed** — but you have to decide what's needed
3. **Compress into a summary** — AI compresses, then passes
sys-context-passing.why:
If you pass everything — at step 5 your input is 100 pages of history. AI reads for 30 seconds, costs as much as a coffee, sometimes doesn't even fit the limit.

If you pass too little — the next step loses context and asks "who is this anyway?".

The right choice depends on the task.
sys-context-passing.when:
Pass EVERYTHING — when there are 2-3 steps and context is small.

Pass ONLY WHAT'S NEEDED — when you have a clear understanding of what each step needs (e.g. step 3 needs only the customer and their plan, the rest doesn't matter).

Use SUMMARY — when context is large and dynamic (long conversations, multi-step research).
sys-context-passing.impact:
Right context = workflow runs in seconds, costs pennies.

Wrong = workflow costs 10× more than it could, sometimes breaks because the input doesn't fit.

Main point: AI gets only what it needs — answers faster and more accurately.
sys-context-passing.example:
Workflow "process a long customer conversation" (50+ messages):

Bad: every step gets the entire history. Step 5 receives 30k words on input, costs $0.50 per request.

Good:
1. Step 1: AI reads the whole conversation → makes a 200-word summary ("customer complains about X, tried Y, ready for Z")
2. Steps 2-5: receive summary + last 5 messages + customer profile
3. Cost drops 20×. Answer quality goes up (AI isn't drowning in noise).
sys-context-passing.mistakes:
Main mistake: "to be safe let's pass everything". Each step ends up slow and expensive, AI gets distracted by irrelevant stuff.

Second mistake: regenerating the summary every time. If context doesn't change — cache the summary and reuse. Otherwise you pay for the same work 10 times.

ai-native-marketing.title: AI for marketing
ai-native-marketing.what:
Marketing = content, campaigns, analytics. Always "do more, check less, deadlines were yesterday". AI here doesn't "write posts for you" — it removes the blank page: gives a first draft in a minute, you finish in your voice in 15 minutes instead of "wrote for 2 hours".

Analytics: instead of "opened 5 dashboards, merged manually" — AI reads the data and says "here's what happened this week, here's a hypothesis about why".
ai-native-marketing.why:
Marketing is always "more content, less budget, faster". AI removes the dilemma "quality vs quantity" — you can have both, if you wire it up correctly.

Main point: AI doesn't replace your brand voice. It gives you a draft in your voice, because you configured it once.
ai-native-marketing.when:
When you notice:
- Content plan exists, execution lags — no hands for drafts
- Each writer writes in their own style, brand voice is fuzzy
- Analytics is done "on Mondays when there's time" — i.e. never
- SEO — theoretically yes, in practice no time
- Campaigns planned 2 weeks ahead, launched in a week — no time to test
ai-native-marketing.impact:
Before: marketing publishes 4 posts a week. After: 12-15 posts at the same quality (AI writes drafts, marketer edits and publishes).

Before: analytics — "let's look at month-end". After: AI sends "yesterday CTR dropped 15%, likely due to creative X, recommend switching to Y" to Slack every morning.

Main point: less "writing by hand", more "deciding what to write and why".

ai-native-marketing.mistakes:
Main mistake: expecting AI to write "as you". It won't. It'll write "similar to you" — your job is to finish.

Second mistake: give the whole team ChatGPT without brand voice setup. You'll get 5 different styles in one brand's posts. First configure AI for the brand voice, then roll out to the team.

Third mistake: automating publishing. AI writes, human looks and clicks "publish" — otherwise sooner or later something embarrassing goes live.

mk-content-ops.title: AI Content Operations
mk-content-ops.what: Content machine on AI: input (brief) → AI draft → human review → publish. Pipeline for blog posts, email, social, documentation. Goal — 10× speedup without losing brand voice.
mk-content-ops.why: Content teams spend 40-60% of time on drafts. AI handles 80% of this work. Freed time goes to strategy, distribution, performance analysis — where AI does not help.
mk-content-ops.when: When the team publishes ≥10 pieces per month. When there is a documented brand voice (or it is easy to assemble). When SEO/audience research exists as brief input.
mk-content-ops.impact: Time-to-publish: 2 days → 4 hours. Content output: +200-300% with the same team. Consistency: single tone across all channels.
mk-content-ops.example:
Content Pipeline:

  Brief (topic + outline + audience)
        ↓
  Project «Blog» with brand voice prompt
        ↓
  AI draft (800 words in 2 minutes)
        ↓
  Quality gate: editor review
        ↓
  Final + SEO optimization
        ↓
  Publish

Metric: 1500-word longread in 4 hours instead of 2 days.
mk-content-ops.mistakes: Doing «AI generates → publish» without a human gate. Any AI text needs review: factcheck, tone, local context. Without human-in-the-loop — generic AI content the reader spots in 3 seconds.

mk-campaign-intel.title: AI Campaign Intelligence
mk-campaign-intel.what: AI support for planning and analyzing marketing campaigns: performance prediction, creative variant generation, post-mortem analysis. AI = «second analyst» on the team.
mk-campaign-intel.why: Campaigns are planned under pressure → reactive decisions, no learning loop. AI adds structured analysis pre-launch (what to try) and post-launch (what worked and why).
mk-campaign-intel.when: Quarterly campaign planning. Before launching a campaign with >$10k budget. Post-mortem after every major campaign. A/B testing copy.
mk-campaign-intel.impact: Campaign ROI: +20-40% thanks to better planning and faster learning. Reduce reactive decisions: 60%.
mk-campaign-intel.example:
Campaign workflow:

  Pre-launch:
  1. AI analyzes past campaigns to similar audience
  2. Generates 5 angle/positioning variants
  3. Predicts likely performance (rough)

  Post-launch:
  1. AI reads all metrics + comments
  2. Pattern-matching: what worked, what did not
  3. Documents learnings in shared knowledge base

After a year: organized library of campaign learnings.
mk-campaign-intel.mistakes: Using AI as «ROI predictor». AI is good at pattern matching historical data, but new markets/channels are beyond its experience. AI = «thoughtful colleague for brainstorming», not «oracle».

mk-brand-voice.title: AI Brand Voice Tuning
mk-brand-voice.what: Documenting and codifying brand voice in the AI generation system. From ad-hoc «we need to sound like us» — to explicit voice guide + system prompts + [[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot examples]] in every Project.
mk-brand-voice.why: Without explicit voice, AI outputs generic «like everyone». With voice guide — text sounds like your team. This is the difference between «AI is noticeable» and «AI is invisible».
mk-brand-voice.when: When team ≥3 people writes content. When «AI tone is not us» complaints. Before AI content operations roll-out to the whole team. When brand vocabulary matters (B2B, tech, lifestyle).
mk-brand-voice.impact: Brand consistency: 60% → 95%. Editor rewrite time: -70%. New team member onboarding: -50%.
mk-brand-voice.example:
Brand Voice Setup:

1. «Voice Guide» document:
   - 3-5 voice attributes (e.g., warm, expert, direct)
   - Do/Don't examples for each
   - 10 sample paragraphs in our style

2. [[node:b-system|System prompt]] in «Blog» Project:
   «You write in style X. Voice attributes: ... Examples: ...»

3. Test: 5 different people give brief → AI generates → blind review → > 80% pick AI-version vs generic.

Real investment: 2-3 days for setup, saves hours per piece.
mk-brand-voice.mistakes: Describing voice abstractly («professional but friendly»). It does not help AI. Voice = examples + concrete attributes + Do/Don't. More concrete, better reproducibility.

mk-seo-optimization.title: AI SEO at Scale
mk-seo-optimization.what: AI for SEO tasks: keyword research, content briefs from SERPs, meta optimization, internal linking. From 1 SEO specialist per 5 content writers — to a team where every writer is SEO-aware.
mk-seo-optimization.why: SEO requires expertise content writers usually do not have. AI closes the gap: author writes, AI checks/suggests SEO improvements. Team moves faster without hiring an SEO spec.
mk-seo-optimization.when: When content output >20 pieces/month + SEO is critical (B2B SaaS, eCommerce, content-driven). When there is budget for keyword research tools (ahrefs/semrush).
mk-seo-optimization.impact: Organic traffic: +30-60% in 6 months. SEO coverage rate (% of pages targeting keywords): 30% → 80%.
mk-seo-optimization.example:
SEO Workflow:

  1. Author writes draft on topic.
  2. AI Step: «here are top-10 SERPs for this topic → what competitors cover, what is missing»
  3. AI Step: «based on this draft + SERP gap analysis, what subtopics to add, what keywords to integrate»
  4. Author redrafts with AI recommendations.
  5. AI Step: meta title + description optimization.

Result: SEO-optimized content without a separate SEO pass.
mk-seo-optimization.mistakes: Trusting AI keyword research fully. AI does not know current trends (cutoff date) and does not see fresh SERPs. Use AI as «SEO advisor», but keyword data — from specialized tools.

mk-performance-analytics.title: AI Marketing Performance Analytics
mk-performance-analytics.what: AI reads marketing metrics (GA, social, email) → writes insight-driven reports with hypotheses and action items. From «here are graphs, figure it out» — to «here is what happened and what we do».
mk-performance-analytics.why: Marketing teams drown in dashboards without actionable insights. AI does the narrative layer: connects dots, explains anomalies, suggests hypotheses. Decision velocity grows.
mk-performance-analytics.when: Weekly/monthly performance reviews. When the team spends >2 hours per week collecting reports. When the «reason» for metric drops is non-obvious.
mk-performance-analytics.impact: Time-to-insight: days → hours. Quality of weekly reviews: structured insights instead of «here are numbers».
mk-performance-analytics.example:
Weekly Marketing Performance Report:

  Inputs:
  - GA4 export (traffic, conversions)
  - Email metrics (open rate, CTR)
  - Social engagement
  - Campaign spend

  AI Output:
  - What grew/dropped (numbers + delta)
  - Hypotheses why (based on past patterns)
  - 3 recommendations for next week
  - Red flags (what needs deeper investigation)

  Human: 15 min validation + 3 decomposed actions.
mk-performance-analytics.mistakes: Using AI as an «attribution engine». AI does not know the real attribution model (multi-touch, view-through). Use AI for narrative and pattern matching, not for exact causation.

mk-team-workflow.title: AI Marketing Team Workflow
mk-team-workflow.what: How a marketing team orchestrates working with AI: shared brand voice, content templates, weekly AI office hours, knowledge sharing. From «everyone with their own Claude» — to a collaborative AI system.
mk-team-workflow.why: Individual usage in marketing does not scale — voice is not consistent, templates duplicate, learnings are lost. Team workflow = single standard + shared library + faster onboarding.
mk-team-workflow.when: Marketing team ≥3 people actively use AI. Inconsistent results emerge. New team members «do not know how we work with AI».
mk-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: +30-50%. New writer time-to-productive: 2 weeks → 3-5 days. Knowledge retention: shared Projects + voice guide = team learns from common mistakes.
mk-team-workflow.example:
Marketing Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project «Marketing Workspace»
2. Files: brand voice guide, content templates, SEO playbook
3. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]: «content rules + naming conventions»
4. Reusable Skills: blog-post-writer, email-drafter, social-snippet
5. Weekly «AI office hours» 30 min: team shows winning prompts, discusses fails
6. Metric: % of content done via shared workflow vs ad-hoc

Stage 3 sign: new writer is productive in 3-5 days, everyone has consistent quality.
mk-team-workflow.mistakes: Making «team workflow» = «one person dictates». Team workflow = collaboration. Each contributor → updates workflow + ownership over one part (voice guide, templates, SEO). Shared ownership = sustainable system.

uc-ai-content-ops-launch.when: When the team already uses AI ad-hoc but quality is inconsistent. When output >10 pieces/month. When there is buy-in from editor/content lead.
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.impact: Outcome: working content pipeline with brand voice in 2 weeks. Metrics: time-to-publish 2 days→4h, brand consistency 60%→90%, content output +200%.

ai-native-customer-support.title: AI for customer support
ai-native-customer-support.what:
Support = 70% routine questions ("where's my invoice", "how to change password", "email not arriving") and 30% real problems. AI closes the routine itself, agents handle only the hard stuff.

This isn't "an annoying chatbot". It's "AI that actually solves the issue in 5 seconds or calls a human if it can't".
ai-native-customer-support.why:
Support is a pain point in any product. Customer base grows → questions grow → you hire more people → budgets burn → agents burn out.

With AI, support stops scaling linearly: 100 customers = 1 agent, 10,000 customers = still 3 agents. Because AI handles 70% of routine.
ai-native-customer-support.when:
When you notice:
- Support team grows faster than customer base
- Agents write the same thing 20 times a day
- Time to first reply > 30 minutes — customers irritated
- Turnover in support — everyone burns out in 6 months
- Knowledge base exists, nobody reads it — easier to ask
ai-native-customer-support.impact:
Before: time to first reply 2 hours, agent handles 40 tickets a day.

After: AI answers routine in 5 seconds (70% of tickets), agent handles 30 complex tickets a day (but more time per one → higher quality).

Customers get answers faster, agents don't burn out on repetition, budget doesn't scale linearly with customer base.

Main point: support stops "plugging holes" and starts "helping customers succeed with the product".
