ai-native-customer-support.mistakes:
Main mistake: "AI will replace support". It won't. AI closes routine, leaving the complex to humans. If you try to fully remove agents — you'll regret it after the first complaint.

Second mistake: not showing what AI says. If the agent can't see what AI told the customer — they'll duplicate, confuse, and damage the relationship. AI should be transparent to the team.

Third mistake: launching AI without escalation. Customer asks the same question 3 times, AI repeats the same answer 3 times — customer livid. You need an explicit "call a human" path.

cs-tier1.title: AI Tier-1 Automation
cs-tier1.what: Automating first-line support: AI reads incoming ticket → finds answer in knowledge base (RAG) → writes a personalized reply → or escalates to a human. Pipeline with explicit quality gates.
cs-tier1.why: 30-50% of all support tickets are repeat questions (password reset, billing, account access). AI closes this mass with consistent quality. Tier-2 agents focus on complex.
cs-tier1.when: Tier-1 volume >100 tickets/week. Structured knowledge base. Clear FAQ categories (40%+ tickets fit into 20 patterns). Buy-in from CS-lead.
cs-tier1.impact: Deflection: 40-60%. Median response time: 4h → 2min for AI-tickets. Tier-2 load drops by 30-40%. CSAT for AI-tickets: 4.2/5 with right setup (vs 4.4 for humans).
cs-tier1.example:
Tier-1 Workflow:

  Incoming ticket
        ↓
  [Classify intent: FAQ vs complex]
   ├─ FAQ → AI processes with KB
   │         ↓
   │     [Confidence > 0.8?]
   │      ├─ Yes → AI response + log
   │      └─ No  → escalate to tier-2 with AI summary
   └─ Complex → directly to human queue

  Quality gate: 10% random AI responses → human review weekly

Metric: deflection rate weekly, CSAT for AI-tickets.
cs-tier1.mistakes: Doing tier-1 at 80% content. Edge cases accumulate: every AI failure = bad experience. Production rule: AI responds only when confidence is high. Otherwise escalate with AI-prepared context for the human.

cs-agent-assist.title: AI Agent Assist
cs-agent-assist.what: AI as a «co-pilot» for tier-2 agent: real-time response suggestions, autocompletion, similar-case search, template generation. Agent stays in the driver seat, AI accelerates.
cs-agent-assist.why: Agent-assist is less risky than tier-1: human is always in the loop. ROI is faster (response time -50% immediately). Team sees AI as «helper», not «threat». Adoption is much higher.
cs-agent-assist.when: Tier-2/3 team spends time writing responses from scratch. There are historical tickets with good answers. Want to raise velocity without quality loss.
cs-agent-assist.impact: Response time per ticket: 8 min → 3 min. Agents handle 50-70% more tickets/day. Quality consistent (AI used as draft, agent edits). New agent onboarding: -50% (AI compensates junior gap).
cs-agent-assist.example:
Agent Assist Setup:

1. Browser plugin or helpdesk integration.
2. Open ticket → AI reads context + customer history.
3. AI suggests:
   - 3 reply variants (formal/friendly/technical)
   - Similar past tickets (resolved)
   - Relevant KB articles
4. Agent selects + edits + sends.
5. AI learns from agent edits (improves suggestions over time).

Real usage: 70% suggestions accepted with minor edits, 20% edited significantly, 10% unused.
cs-agent-assist.mistakes: Forcing agents to use AI «mandatorily». If a suggestion is bad — it forces writing from scratch. Drive adoption through value (show time saved per ticket), not mandate.

cs-knowledge-base.title: AI Knowledge Base Operations
cs-knowledge-base.what: Knowledge base turns from «PDF dump» into a living AI system: vector search, auto-updates based on resolved tickets, gap analysis (what is often asked but no article exists), structured taxonomy.
cs-knowledge-base.why: Without a good KB, all AI support fails. KB = single source of truth for AI. KB quality ≠ article count. Quality KB ops = more impact than just launching AI.
cs-knowledge-base.when: In parallel with tier-1 setup. When AI bot answers «I do not know» to >20% of questions. When agents complain «cannot find the article». When KB has not been updated in >6 months.
cs-knowledge-base.impact: KB findability: 50% → 90% (vector search vs keyword). AI deflection rate grows +15-20% (more coverage). Agent onboarding: -40% time.
cs-knowledge-base.example:
KB Ops Pipeline:

Weekly:
  1. AI reads resolved tickets for the week.
  2. Identifies frequent questions without KB articles.
  3. Drafts new KB articles from ticket solutions.
  4. KB editor reviews + publishes.

Monthly:
  1. AI analyzes KB usage (which articles cited).
  2. Flags outdated content (product changed, article did not).
  3. Suggests merges (duplicate articles).

Metric: % of tickets where AI found KB match → up over time.
cs-knowledge-base.mistakes: Making KB only for humans. Modern KB optimization = for AI + humans. Structure (clear headers, atomic articles, metadata) matters for AI retrieval. Otherwise AI does not find — even if the article exists.

cs-escalation.title: AI Escalation Intelligence
cs-escalation.what: Smart escalation: AI decides when to hand off to a human and exactly to whom (by specialization, load, severity). Plus prepares escalation context — the agent gets not «here is a ticket», but «here is a ticket + history + what AI tried».
cs-escalation.why: Dumb escalation = ticket arrives without context, agent spends 5 minutes reading. Smart = agent sees summary + what was already tried + recommended next step. Velocity grows without quality loss.
cs-escalation.when: When tier-1 AI is running and tier-2 routing is needed. When there are specializations (billing vs technical vs account). When escalation is a bottleneck.
cs-escalation.impact: Time-to-resolution for escalated tickets: -40%. Routing accuracy: 80% → 95% (correct specialist on first try). Agent satisfaction +: less «why did they pass this to me».
cs-escalation.example:
Escalation Workflow:

  AI cannot resolve ticket
        ↓
  [Classify problem domain]
   ├─ Billing → queue: billing_team
   ├─ Technical → queue: tech_support
   └─ Account → queue: account_specialists
        ↓
  AI prepares escalation summary:
   - Customer info + history
   - What customer wants
   - What AI tried (and why it didn't work)
   - Suggested next step
        ↓
  Agent picks up: context ready in 30 sec instead of 5 min.

Metric: agent feedback on escalation quality.
cs-escalation.mistakes: Escalating «just in case» at low confidence. If AI errs 10% but escalates 50% — it is degradation. Calibrate threshold: too high = killed deflection, too low = bad quality.

cs-quality-monitoring.title: AI Quality Monitoring
cs-quality-monitoring.what: Continuous monitoring of AI response quality: weekly sample → human review → identify failure patterns → adjust prompts/KB. Without monitoring, AI degrades silently: errors accumulate, no one sees.
cs-quality-monitoring.why: AI is not static: KB changes, product changes, customer questions change. AI that worked in Q1 may slip in Q3. Quality monitoring catches drift before CSAT drops.
cs-quality-monitoring.when: From day 1 of AI tier-1 launch. Mandatory. Not «when there is a problem» — continuous. Minimum: 10% AI responses random sample → weekly review.
cs-quality-monitoring.impact: AI drift detection: before customers notice (CSAT does not drop). Continuous improvement: every week prompts/KB get better. Trust in the AI system grows through explicit quality data.
cs-quality-monitoring.example:
Quality Monitoring Process:

Weekly:
  1. Random sample 10% of AI responses.
  2. Quality team rates: accuracy, tone, completeness.
  3. Failure patterns extracted: «AI confuses billing X with Y», «misses context Z».
  4. Action: update KB articles OR adjust [[node:b-system|system prompt]] OR add edge case to training data.

Metric:
  - % AI responses rated >4/5
  - Trending direction (better/worse week-over-week)
  - Top 3 failure categories

Escalation: if quality < 4/5 for 2 weeks → pause AI tier-1, investigate.
cs-quality-monitoring.mistakes: Monitoring without action loop. If found errors do not lead to changes — it is theater. Quality monitoring must be embedded in weekly product process (Mon: review, Tue: fix, Wed: validate, ...).

cs-support-analytics.title: AI Support Analytics
cs-support-analytics.what: AI reads support metrics + ticket content → writes insight reports: trending issues, customer sentiment, agent performance patterns, product feedback. Turns support data into product insights.
cs-support-analytics.why: Support is free user research. Thousands of conversations with real customers. But the team drowns in objects/dashboards. AI does the narrative layer + connects to product/marketing teams.
cs-support-analytics.when: Weekly support reviews. When product team wants «voice of customer». When there is a pattern «many complaints about feature X» — need systematic detection.
cs-support-analytics.impact: Time-to-insight: days → hours. Product team gets trending issues automatically. Customer voice loop closes: from ticket → insight → product change → fewer tickets.
cs-support-analytics.example:
Weekly Support Analytics Report:

  Inputs:
  - All tickets for the week (resolved + open)
  - CSAT scores + comments
  - Agent performance metrics
  - Product release notes

  AI Output:
  - Top 5 trending issues (with ticket count + delta)
  - Sentiment analysis: where customers are frustrated
  - Correlation: «new feature X released → tickets about X +40%»
  - Recommendations for product team
  - Recommendations for KB updates

Distribution: report shared with product + marketing → closing the loop.
cs-support-analytics.mistakes: Doing support analytics in isolation. If insights do not reach product/engineering — they are useless. Set up explicit channels: weekly «Support Insights» Slack post in #product, monthly review session.

cs-team-workflow.title: AI Customer Support Team Workflow
cs-team-workflow.what: CS team operating model with AI: shared knowledge base ops, common agent-assist setup, AI office hours, quality calibration sessions, AI-aware promotion path for agents. From «AI = a tool» — to «AI = part of how we operate».
cs-team-workflow.why: Individual AI usage in support does not work — consistency for customers is needed (everyone gets same quality answer). Team workflow ensures this through shared setup + processes.
cs-team-workflow.when: When team ≥5 agents use AI. When new agents arrive and «do not know how». When quality is inconsistent between shift teams.
cs-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: agents process 50%+ more tickets. New agent onboarding: 4 weeks → 2 weeks. Quality consistency across shifts: +60%. AI literacy team-wide.
cs-team-workflow.example:
CS Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project «Support Workspace»:
   - KB indexed
   - Brand voice guide (tone for customers)
   - Common scenarios templates

2. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]: response guidelines, escalation criteria, tone rules.

3. Skills: response-drafter, ticket-summarizer, escalation-formatter.

4. Weekly calibration: team reviews 5 AI-handled tickets together. Discusses: what worked, what would change.

5. AI-aware promotion: agents who improve AI workflow → senior path (not just «answer more tickets»).

Result: team functions as a cohesive AI-augmented unit.
cs-team-workflow.mistakes: Treating AI usage as «individual perk». Without team-level workflow, customers get inconsistent experience (depending on which agent picks). AI = team capability, not individual skill.

uc-ai-support-tier1.title: Launch AI Tier-1 Support
uc-ai-support-tier1.what: Full path from «all by hand» to «AI closes 40% of tickets». Cross-layer path through 7 nodes: Foundation → [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI Fundamentals]] → Systems → Transformation.
uc-ai-support-tier1.why: Tier-1 automation = highest-ROI AI project in support. This UC shows a structured approach (not «buy a bot»): KB first, then AI, then quality monitoring.
uc-ai-support-tier1.when: Tier-1 volume >100 tickets/week. Baseline CSAT exists for comparison. Can invest 3-4 weeks in setup. Buy-in from CS-lead AND product (for KB).
uc-ai-support-tier1.impact: Outcome: working tier-1 AI with 40% deflection in 4 weeks. Metrics: deflection rate 0→40%, median response time 4h→2min for AI-tickets, CSAT maintained at baseline.
uc-ai-support-tier1.example:
Path (7 steps):

Week 1: Knowledge Base prep.
1. Foundation: af-rag-basics → understand what RAG needs
2. Foundation: af-vector-db → vector DB choice (pgvector usually enough)
3. Systems: sys-rag-architecture → pattern choice (Advanced RAG mandatory)
4. Audit + restructure existing KB articles

Week 2: AI tier-1 setup.
5. Foundation: prompting → [[node:b-system|system prompt]] for support bot
6. Foundation: projects → create «Support Bot» Project with KB
7. Transformation: cs-tier1 → build workflow with quality gates

Week 3: Quality + escalation.
8. Transformation: cs-escalation → correct routing for escalations
9. Transformation: cs-quality-monitoring → setup random sample review

Week 4: Roll-out.
10. Pilot on 1 ticket category. Measure deflection + CSAT.
11. Expand to 3-5 categories. Iterate.

Stage transition: 1→2.
uc-ai-support-tier1.mistakes: Launching AI tier-1 without KB ops first. If the KB is not suitable for AI retrieval (bad structure, outdated) — AI will answer generic or wrong. KB ops = 50% of UC work. Do not skip.

ai-native-product.title: AI for product teams
ai-native-product.what:
A product manager spends 50% of time "gathering insights": customer interviews, feedback from support, analytics data, stakeholder tickets. And 50% on "making a decision and writing it up".

AI speeds up the first half by 5×: reads interviews, aggregates feedback, finds patterns. PM has time left for strategy.
ai-native-product.why:
Product work is "lots of noise, little signal". AI is good at separating one from the other: from 200 feedbacks it pulls out 5 real themes, from 30 interviews — 3 stable insights.

Main point: PM stops being a "feedback-tool operator" and becomes "the person who makes decisions".
ai-native-product.when:
When you notice:
- 30 customer interviews and you haven't read them yet
- 200 feedbacks from support in Notion — synthesis "someday"
- Roadmap built by "loudness", not by data
- Spending an hour every morning on "what happened in the product yesterday"
- Specs take 3 days — then a week of revisions
ai-native-product.impact:
Before: 30 customer interviews = a month of synthesis, by the end you've forgotten the first ones.

After: AI does the first-pass synthesis in 2 hours, PM verifies and digs into the important parts → 3 days instead of a month.

Before: PRD takes a week to write, a week to review.

After: AI drafts in 30 minutes from a brief, PM revises for 2 days, reviewers get a clean document.

Main point: PM works on "what's important to do", not on "how to gather data".

ai-native-product.mistakes:
Main mistake: letting AI make product decisions. AI is good at data synthesis, but "what matters more" is your job. If AI says "build X" and you build it without your own analysis — you'll blame AI when it doesn't work out.

Second mistake: automating interviews without a human. AI does the interview, AI processes it, AI decides what's important — you'll get what you already knew. Live interviews with a human are mandatory. AI speeds up processing, not replacement.

Third mistake: trusting AI "without verification". AI can hallucinate insights that aren't in the data. Always verify key conclusions against the original sources.

pd-discovery-research.title: AI Discovery Research
pd-discovery-research.what: AI-powered user research: automatic interview synthesis, competitive analysis, market research. From «read 20 interviews in 3 days» — to «AI extracts themes in an hour, PM validates».
pd-discovery-research.why: Discovery is the most time-intensive part of PM work. 50 interviews = a week of manual synthesis. AI does a first pass in an hour, the PM focuses on validation and interpretation.
pd-discovery-research.when: When there are >10 interviews/customer calls on one topic. When quarterly customer research is needed. When the competitive landscape changes and you need to track it.
pd-discovery-research.impact: Time-to-insight: days → hours. Coverage: PM can «process» 50 interviews instead of 10. Quality: structured themes instead of «here are my notes».
pd-discovery-research.example:
Research Synthesis Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - 30 interview transcripts
  - Customer support tickets (1 month)
  - Competitor reviews on G2/Trustpilot
        ↓
  Project «Research» with RAG index
        ↓
  AI Steps:
  1. Extract themes (frequency + sentiment)
  2. Cluster similar quotes
  3. Identify gaps (what people often mention but we do not do)
  4. Generate hypothesis matrix
        ↓
  PM validates: which themes are actionable, which need follow-up
        ↓
  Output: structured research report + raw data accessible

Metric: time-to-insight, theme coverage.
pd-discovery-research.mistakes: Relying on AI without human validation. AI misses nuance: irony, edge cases, cultural context. Workflow: AI extracts → PM validates a 10-20% sample → confidence in the rest grows. Without validation — false insights.

pd-spec-generation.title: AI Spec Generation
pd-spec-generation.what: AI writes PRDs, user stories, technical specs from a rough idea + research input. From «PM sits for 2 days writing a PRD» — to «PM iterates with AI for 2 hours, draft is ready».
pd-spec-generation.why: PRD writing is a shipping bottleneck. PMs spend days formatting/structuring what they already know in their heads. AI handles the «writing» part, the PM focuses on content quality.
pd-spec-generation.when: When the team loses momentum between «have an idea» and «PRD written». When there is a documented PRD template. When rough notes / research are already on hand.
pd-spec-generation.impact: Time-to-PRD: 2 days → 4 hours (including iterations). Consistency: a single format for all specs. Quality: AI catches missing sections (success metrics, edge cases, etc.).
pd-spec-generation.example:
Spec Generation Workflow:

  Input for AI:
  - Rough idea (3-5 sentences from PM)
  - Research output (from pd-discovery)
  - Existing PRD template + 2-3 high-quality examples
        ↓
  AI generates:
  - Problem statement
  - User stories with acceptance criteria
  - Success metrics proposals
  - Open questions
  - Technical considerations (for engineering)
        ↓
  PM iterates: 3-5 rounds of edits
        ↓
  Output: ship-ready PRD

Metric: time-to-spec, dev team feedback on PRD quality.
pd-spec-generation.mistakes: Doing AI-PRDs without research input. «Write a PRD for feature X» = generic stuff. Quality output requires quality input: research, examples, constraints. Garbage in = garbage out.

pd-roadmap-intelligence.title: AI Roadmap Intelligence
pd-roadmap-intelligence.what: AI helps with roadmap prioritization: analyzing feedback patterns, competitor moves, customer requests, internal data → ranked priorities with reasoning. AI = «second analyst» in roadmap discussions.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.why: Roadmap prioritization is usually done «by gut» under stakeholder pressure. AI brings a structured framework: explicit weights, data-based scoring, consideration of alternatives.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.when: Quarterly planning. Before a roadmap review with executives. When «everyone has their own opinion» and a structured framework is needed for the decision.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.impact: Reactive prioritization: -60%. Stakeholder alignment: faster (data, not opinions). Roadmap thrashing: reduced (explicit criteria prevent frequent changes).
pd-roadmap-intelligence.example:
Roadmap Prioritization Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - All product opportunities (backlog + new ideas)
  - Customer feedback themes (from feedback-synthesis)
  - Competitor analysis
  - Internal metrics (revenue impact, retention)
  - Strategic objectives (current quarter)
        ↓
  AI Scoring:
  - Each opportunity rated on: impact, effort, strategic fit, risk
  - Reasoning explicit for each
  - Alternative orderings played out
        ↓
  PM + leadership: review AI ranking + override based on judgment
        ↓
  Output: prioritized roadmap with documented reasoning

Value: next quarter you CAN explain «why we chose this».
pd-roadmap-intelligence.mistakes: Accepting AI roadmap as final. AI scoring is based on the data you gave — but it does not know board politics, executive priorities, or upcoming launches. AI = input into a decision, not the decision itself.

pd-experimentation.title: AI Feature Experimentation
pd-experimentation.what: AI support for A/B testing: hypothesis generation, variant design, statistical analysis interpretation, learnings synthesis. From «ran A/B, forgot results» — to «structured experimentation engine».
pd-experimentation.why: Most teams run A/B tests poorly: weak hypotheses, no power analysis, results forgotten. AI structures this: forces explicit hypothesis, generates variant ideas, helps interpret results.
pd-experimentation.when: When the team runs ≥3 experiments per quarter. When experiment outputs do not turn into product knowledge. When you need to scale experimentation across multiple teams.
pd-experimentation.impact: Experiment velocity: +50%. Experiments with clear learnings: 50% → 90%. Knowledge retention: structured library of experiment outcomes.
pd-experimentation.example:
Experimentation Workflow:

  1. Hypothesis Generation:
     - PM inputs: «hypothesis: shorter onboarding → higher activation»
     - AI critiques: «specify metric, magnitude, timeframe, sample needed»
     - Result: «If we cut onboarding from 5 to 2 steps, activation rate +15% over 4 weeks (n>1000)»

  2. Variant Design:
     - AI generates 3-5 specific variant approaches
     - Discusses pros/cons of each

  3. Post-experiment Analysis:
     - Input: results data
     - AI: «winner with X confidence. Caveats: ... Recommended follow-up: ...»

  4. Library:
     - AI maintains experiment knowledge base
     - Search: «did we try X before?»

Metric: experiments per quarter, learnings library size.
pd-experimentation.mistakes: Using AI for «predict before run». AI cannot predict the result of an A/B (if it could — an A/B would not be needed). AI is good at: hypothesis sharpening, variant ideation, post-analysis interpretation. Not predictive.

pd-feedback-synthesis.title: AI Feedback Synthesis
pd-feedback-synthesis.what: AI reads all user feedback (NPS comments, support tickets, reviews, sales notes) → structured insights with trends. From «PM read ~50 comments» — to «AI processed 5000 and found patterns».
pd-feedback-synthesis.why: Customer feedback is fragmented across 5-10 sources. The PM physically cannot read everything. AI does aggregation + synthesis. Sentiment shifts visible before they show up in churn.
pd-feedback-synthesis.when: When there are ≥3 feedback sources (NPS, support, reviews, sales calls, social). When the product team wants «voice of customer» systematic, not anecdotal.
pd-feedback-synthesis.impact: Coverage: 5% of feedback is read → 100% is processed. Time-to-trend: 2 months → 2 weeks. Decision quality: data-backed instead of «I remember someone complained».
pd-feedback-synthesis.example:
**Feedback synthesis pipeline:**

**1. Sources (weekly):**
- NPS responses (quarterly × 1000+)
- Support tickets with CSAT comments
- App Store / G2 reviews
- Sales call notes
- Social mentions

**2. AI processing:**
- Clean + dedupe
- Categorize (feature, UX, pricing, performance, ...)
- Sentiment analysis
- Theme extraction
- Trend detection (week-over-week)

**3. Weekly output:**
- Top 5 themes (with magnitude + delta)
- Quote samples for each
- Critical issues to investigate

**4. Distribution:**
- Product team → decisions
- Engineering → bug themes
- Marketing → positioning themes

**Metrics:** feedback coverage, time-to-action on trending issues.
pd-feedback-synthesis.mistakes: Doing feedback synthesis in a vacuum. Output must flow into roadmap planning, not into a read-only report. Workflow: synthesis → product review → roadmap update → measure impact. Without the loop — polite theater.

pd-product-analytics.title: AI Product Analytics
pd-product-analytics.what: AI reads product usage data (Amplitude, Mixpanel, GA) → writes insight reports with hypotheses «why did this happen?» and suggested investigations. From «here is a dashboard» — to «here is what happened and what it means».
pd-product-analytics.why: Product analytics tools show «what happened», but not «why». PM/analytics manager spends hours on formulating hypotheses. AI does this first-pass, the human verifies.
pd-product-analytics.when: Weekly product reviews. After every major release. When a metric is unexpected (growth or drop). When the team «does not understand why» something is happening.
pd-product-analytics.impact: Time-to-hypothesis: days → hours. Coverage: analytics-aware decisions grow from 30% to 70%+ of the team.
pd-product-analytics.example:
Weekly Product Analytics Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - Top-line metrics (DAU, MAU, retention, activation)
  - Feature usage (new + existing)
  - User segments behavior
  - Recent product releases
        ↓
  AI Analysis:
  1. What changed (numbers + delta + significance)
  2. Correlation: «release X → metric Y +Z%»
  3. Anomaly detection (unusual segment behavior)
  4. Hypotheses (ranked by likelihood)
  5. Recommended investigations (queries to run, segments to look at)
        ↓
  Product team:
  - Validates top hypotheses
  - Decides actions
  - Adds learnings to knowledge base

Metric: % of metric changes with documented explanation.
pd-product-analytics.mistakes: Trusting AI causal claims. «Release X caused metric Y +5%» — that is correlation, not causation. AI recommends a hypothesis, the human must validate via proper analysis (cohort, A/B, before-after).

pd-team-workflow.title: AI Product Team Workflow
pd-team-workflow.what: Product team operating model with AI: shared research workspace, common spec templates, feedback synthesis pipeline, weekly AI office hours. From «every PM with their own Claude» — to a «collaborative AI-powered product team».
pd-team-workflow.why: Individual usage in product does not scale — research findings are lost between PMs, specs are inconsistent, knowledge is not shared. Team workflow creates a shared institutional memory.
pd-team-workflow.when: Product team ≥3 PMs use AI. When «everyone has their own approach to specs». When research findings are lost after launch. When a new PM «does not know how we work».
pd-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: +30%. New PM onboarding: 6 weeks → 3 weeks (via shared knowledge). Decision quality: improves over time (institutional memory grows).
pd-team-workflow.example:
Product Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project «Product Workspace»:
   - All research transcripts indexed
   - Past PRDs library
   - Experiment learnings
   - Customer feedback (categorized)

2. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]: writing conventions, PRD template, decision frameworks.

3. Skills:
   - research-synthesizer
   - prd-drafter
   - feedback-categorizer
   - experiment-designer

4. Weekly «AI office hours» 30 min:
   - Best prompt discoveries
   - Failed AI experiments (what is not working)
   - Cross-team learning

5. Quarterly knowledge curation:
   - What to add to shared workspace
   - What is outdated and to remove

Stage 3 sign: new PM writes a shipping-ready PRD by the end of the first month.
pd-team-workflow.mistakes: Doing team workflow without a librarian role. Shared workspace without maintainership = junk drawer in 6 months. Someone must curate: weekly review of new content, monthly cleanup of outdated.

uc-ai-discovery-launch.title: Launch AI Discovery
uc-ai-discovery-launch.what: Full path from «doing research by hand» to «AI-powered discovery pipeline». Cross-layer path through 6 nodes: Foundation → Systems → Transformation.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.why: The most common product team request: «we have tons of interviews / feedback / research, but synthesis is a bottleneck». This UC solves it systematically via RAG + workflows + product practices.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.when: When the product team has ≥30 interviews or ≥100 feedback items without structured processing. When the discovery → ship cycle is slow. When there is buy-in from Head of Product.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.impact: Outcome: working AI-discovery pipeline in 2 weeks. Metrics: time-to-insight ≤2 hours per topic, research coverage 100% (vs 30% manually), structured theme extraction.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.example:
Path (6 steps):

Week 1: Setup foundation.
1. Foundation: prompting → how to formulate synthesis prompts
2. Foundation: af-rag-basics → RAG basics for research repository
3. Foundation: projects → create «Discovery Workspace» with research files

Week 1-2: Build pipeline.
4. Systems: sys-context-passing → properly pass research context between steps
5. Transformation: pd-discovery-research → concrete workflow with PM validation gates

Week 2: Extend & sustain.
6. Transformation: pd-feedback-synthesis → extend to ongoing feedback (not just interviews)

Day 1-3: Index existing research in the Project. Test synthesis on 5-10 interviews.
Day 4-7: Refine prompts based on validation feedback. Document patterns.
Day 8-14: Scale to the full research backlog. Train other PMs.

Stage transition: 1→2.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.mistakes: Doing a UC without structured research input. If interviews are scattered chaotically across Notion / Google Docs / Slack — AI cannot find them. Day 1 work = organize the research repository. This is 30% of UC time. Do not skip.

ai-native-enterprise.title: AI transformation for the whole company
ai-native-enterprise.what:
A section for leaders (CTO, CIO, Head of Transformation): how to roll out AI not just "in marketing" but across a 200+ person company. Strategy, change management, governance, ROI, risks.

This isn't "buy ChatGPT licenses". It's "how to make AI the way of working, not a toy in the corner".
ai-native-enterprise.why:
A big company doesn't turn AI-native in a month. It's 1-3 years of work on strategy, teams, culture and processes. Without a systematic approach — the rollout dies halfway.

This section is a map of typical transformation tasks and a warning about the rakes 80% of companies step on.
ai-native-enterprise.when:
When:
- You're a CTO/CIO at a 100+ person company and need to prepare an AI strategy
- The board asked "what's our AI story" — you need a clear answer
- You already have 5 AI pilots in different departments, but they're disconnected
- Competitors are pulling ahead — you need to catch up systematically
- You launched AI pilots — nobody uses them → need to understand why
ai-native-enterprise.impact:
Without a system: 20 pilots, 3 alive, 17 abandoned. Teams disillusioned, budget wasted.

With a system: 5 directions prioritized, 4 driven to production, measurable quarterly ROI, teams see results and want more.

Main point: AI stops being a "fashionable toy" and becomes a real way of working.

ai-native-enterprise.mistakes:
Main mistake: "push AI from the top". "Everyone now works with AI" in a CEO email — 2 weeks later everyone's back to old ways. You need bottom-up momentum from teams + top-down support.

Second mistake: measuring ROI "in 6 months". By then the project is forgotten. Measure small wins every 2-4 weeks (that's how people believe and back it).

Third mistake: not investing in training. Bought licenses, forgot the team → licenses sit idle → ROI zero. Tooling budget ≤ training budget.

en-transformation-strategy.title: AI Transformation Strategy
en-transformation-strategy.what: A document-based AI strategy for 12-24 months: vision, north-star metrics, sequencing of initiatives, investment thesis, success criteria. Not «let us use AI», but «here is HOW we win from AI».
en-transformation-strategy.why: Without explicit strategy, AI initiatives = different departments doing different things. With strategy — coordination, leverage between departments, clear priorities. Strategy doc = alignment tool for leadership.
en-transformation-strategy.when: After 6-12 months of successful pilots in several departments. When the board asks questions about AI ROI. Before annual planning. When you need to hire an AI lead.
en-transformation-strategy.impact: Decision velocity: 3× faster on AI-related decisions. Org alignment: leadership team on the same page (literally). Time-to-execution: tactical teams understand priorities in days, not months.
en-transformation-strategy.example:
AI Transformation Strategy doc (8-12 pages):

1. Vision (1 page): where the company is in 2 years with AI
2. North-star metrics (3-5): cost reduction, revenue growth, NPS, talent retention
3. Strategic bets (3-7): «Stage-by-stage AI in customer support», «AI-augmented product development», ...
4. Sequencing: what we do Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4
5. Investment thesis: where we spend, where we save
6. Risk & governance principles
7. Success criteria + checkpoints

Creation process: 2-3 weeks with executives + tactical leads. Reviewed quarterly.

Metric: % of strategic decisions referencing the doc (target: >80% in 6 months).
en-transformation-strategy.mistakes: Making a strategy doc «once and forgotten». The AI landscape changes every 6 months — the strategy must refresh quarterly. And: not making just vision without metrics. Strategy without measurable outcomes = wish list.

en-change-management.title: AI Change Management
en-change-management.what: Structured approach to changing team behaviors under AI-native operations: communication, training, role evolution, resistance management. Tech adoption ≠ change management — these are different disciplines.
en-change-management.why: The most common cause of failed AI initiatives is not tech, but adoption. Teams fear (job loss), do not believe (saw hype before), do not know (skills gap). Change management addresses this explicitly.
en-change-management.when: Before rolling out a tactical direction to the full team. When the first pilots work but adoption stalls. When there is an «AI champions» vs «AI skeptics» split on the team.
en-change-management.impact: Adoption rate: 30% → 80% with proper change mgmt. Resistance reduced (not eliminated). Skills gap closes via structured training. Time-to-Stage 3: -50% for tactical directions.
en-change-management.example:
Change Management Framework (for one tactical direction):

Phase 1: Awareness (week 1-2)
  - All-hands: «here is what we are doing + why»
  - Q&A sessions: address concerns openly
  - Champions identification

Phase 2: Education (week 3-4)
  - Hands-on workshops for everyone
  - Skill development: 10 hours of structured learning
  - Champions trained deeper

Phase 3: Adoption (week 5-12)
  - Pilot teams using daily
  - Office hours for help
  - Wins shared widely

Phase 4: Reinforcement (ongoing)
  - Promotion criteria include AI usage
  - Career path for «AI-augmented» roles
  - Continuous learning culture

Metric: % of team actively using AI weekly.
en-change-management.mistakes: Thinking that training = change management. Training is skill transfer. Change mgmt is behavioral shift. Without the second, the first = waste. And: not answering «will I lose my job?». Avoiding it = doubt grows.

en-governance.title: AI Governance
en-governance.what: Set of rules and processes governing how AI is used in the organization: data privacy, model selection, output validation, vendor management, compliance. Not «security team forbids» — but «structured framework for responsible use».
en-governance.why: Without governance, compliance gaps accumulate: data leaks via AI inputs, customer data in third-party models, audit trail missing. Regulatory landscape (GDPR, EU AI Act) tightens — better get ahead.
en-governance.when: Before production AI use cases (NOT after). When there is customer data, financial data, PII in AI flows. When multiple departments use different AI tools.
en-governance.impact: Compliance: prevented incidents. Trust: customers trust AI products. Speed: clear rules speed up decision-making (no «can we or can we not?» discussions). Risk reduction quantifiable.
en-governance.example:
AI Governance Framework:

1. Data classification: what can/cannot go into AI flows
   - Public data: any AI tool
   - Internal data: approved enterprise tools only
   - Customer data: with consent + data residency check
   - PII: encrypted + DPA in place

2. Vendor management:
   - Approved AI tools list (updated quarterly)
   - DPA requirements
   - Audit logs

3. Output validation:
   - Human review for customer-facing AI outputs
   - Quality monitoring (statistical)
   - Bias testing

4. Incident response:
   - AI-specific incident playbook
   - Reporting channels

Reviewed: quarterly + after any incident.

Metric: incidents per quarter (target: 0 high-severity).
en-governance.mistakes: Doing governance as a «list of prohibitions». Governance works as an enabler if framed as «here is how to do this responsibly». Without enablement framing — shadow AI usage (teams use unauthorized tools).

en-coe.title: AI Center of Excellence
en-coe.what: Central team (3-10 people) — AI lead, ML engineers, AI ethicists, product manager — supporting tactical teams: best practices, shared infrastructure, training, governance liaison. Not building everything, but enabling others.
en-coe.why: Without a CoE, each tactical team reinvents the wheel: discovers RAG, learns prompt engineering, sets up vector DB. CoE shares this knowledge and infrastructure → 5-10× faster for all subsequent teams.
en-coe.when: After 2-3 successful tactical AI directions. When «how and where do I find an AI expert?» becomes a regular question. When signing up for enterprise AI vendors (CoE manages).
en-coe.impact: New AI initiative time-to-launch: 6 months → 2 months. Cost: shared infra cheaper than per-team setup. Quality: best practices spread. Career: clear AI path for talent.
en-coe.example:
CoE Structure:

Core team (3-5):
  - Head of AI / Chief AI Officer
  - Senior ML/AI engineer
  - AI Product Manager
  - AI Ethics & Governance lead

Functions:
  1. Shared infrastructure (vector DBs, LLM API contracts, monitoring)
  2. Best practices library ([[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] templates, Skills, patterns)
  3. Office hours (weekly, anyone can attend)
  4. Training programs (3 levels: foundational, intermediate, advanced)
  5. Tooling decisions (which AI tools company-wide)
  6. Governance coordination (with security/legal)
  7. Talent: hiring AI roles + upskilling existing
  8. Showcase: monthly «AI demos» across the company

Key metric: CoE-enabled launches per quarter.
en-coe.mistakes: Making CoE «the AI department» — building everything. CoE = enablement, not execution. Tactical teams build, CoE shares know-how. Otherwise CoE becomes a bottleneck.

en-roi-measurement.title: AI ROI Measurement
en-roi-measurement.what: Framework for measuring AI investment returns: cost vs value, attribution to AI vs other factors, leading vs lagging indicators, payback period. Turns «AI saves time» into «AI saved $X this quarter».
en-roi-measurement.why: Without ROI measurement, AI initiatives ride on vibes. When finance asks «show me the money?», the response should be quantified. ROI measurement = sustainable AI program longevity.
en-roi-measurement.when: After 3-6 months of AI in production. Before budget planning (annual or quarterly). When executives ask about AI value. When you need to prioritize between AI initiatives.
en-roi-measurement.impact: Budget approval: 2× faster for AI initiatives with tracked ROI. Resource allocation: efficient (kill failing, double on winning). Stakeholder confidence: high.
en-roi-measurement.example:
AI ROI Framework:

Cost side:
  - Direct: AI API costs, tools, infrastructure
  - Indirect: training time, change management, governance overhead
  - Hidden: opportunity cost of team time

Value side:
  - Time saved (× hourly cost of saved roles)
  - Quality improvement (cost of errors avoided)
  - Revenue generated (new capabilities)
  - Risk reduction (compliance, incidents avoided)
  - Customer satisfaction (retention impact)

Attribution: how to know AI caused this?
  - Before/after comparison + control group when possible
  - A/B testing on features
  - Counterfactual analysis for high-stakes claims

Reporting:
  - Monthly per tactical direction
  - Quarterly aggregate to leadership
  - Annual: full impact report

Metric: documented ROI per initiative > 3× cost (target).
en-roi-measurement.mistakes: Counting only cost savings, ignoring intangibles. AI brings not only time — but capability gains, morale, future optionality. Without holistic ROI — value undervalued, program cancelled prematurely.

en-risk-management.title: AI Risk Management
en-risk-management.what: Systematic identification, assessment, mitigation of AI-specific risks: hallucinations in production, model drift, data leaks, regulatory non-compliance, bias, vendor dependencies. Risk awareness, not risk avoidance.
en-risk-management.why: AI risks differ from traditional IT risks: probabilistic, evolving, often invisible until late. Traditional risk frameworks do not catch them. Need an AI-specific approach.
en-risk-management.when: From day 1 of every AI initiative (NOT after an incident). Before production launch. Annually for existing AI systems. After any notable industry incident.
en-risk-management.impact: High-severity incidents: 0 prevented to occurred (best outcome). Insurance cost: lower with documented program. Regulatory readiness: ahead of EU AI Act, NIST framework.
en-risk-management.example:
AI Risk Categories + Mitigations:

1. Hallucinations:
   - Risk: AI returns wrong info confidently
   - Mitigation: RAG with citations, human review for customer-facing, quality monitoring

2. Model drift:
   - Risk: AI behavior changes without notice (model update, data shift)
   - Mitigation: continuous quality monitoring, golden test sets, rollback ability

3. Data leaks:
   - Risk: customer/sensitive data in model providers
   - Mitigation: data classification, approved vendors, encryption, audit logs

4. Bias:
   - Risk: AI discriminates (hiring, pricing, content)
   - Mitigation: bias testing, diverse training data, monitoring by demographic

5. Regulatory:
   - Risk: GDPR, EU AI Act, sector-specific violations
   - Mitigation: compliance review per use case, legal sign-off, documentation

6. Vendor lock:
   - Risk: depends entirely on one AI provider
   - Mitigation: abstraction layer, multi-vendor strategy, internal fallback

Risk register: updated quarterly.

Metric: identified vs occurred risks (catch rate target: >90%).
en-risk-management.mistakes: Thinking risk management = compliance checklist. Real AI risk management = thinking about edge cases, scenarios, second-order effects. Checklist alone — false security.

en-talent-strategy.title: AI Talent Strategy
en-talent-strategy.what: Approach to building AI capability on the team: hiring AI roles, upskilling existing employees, retention in the AI-talent market, career paths for AI-augmented roles. Talent is the hardest part for long-term AI success.
en-talent-strategy.why: AI tools are commodity, AI talent is not. Companies without a talent strategy lose people to Big Tech. Companies with a good strategy attract top talent, retain existing employees via growth opportunities.
en-talent-strategy.when: Continuously (not «one time»). Before every tactical direction launch. When scaling the AI program. When attrition in AI-relevant roles rises.
en-talent-strategy.impact: AI talent retention: 90%+ (vs 60% industry average). Time-to-fill AI roles: 2× faster (employer brand). Internal mobility: 30%+ move into AI-augmented roles.
en-talent-strategy.example:
AI Talent Strategy:

1. Hiring framework:
   - Roles needed: ML engineers, AI PMs, AI ethicists, prompt engineers
   - Compensation benchmarks (AI talent premium)
   - Sourcing channels (universities, conferences, community)

2. Upskilling:
   - 3 levels: foundational (everyone), intermediate (heavy users), advanced (builders)
   - Time budget: 4-8 hours/month protected learning time
   - Recognition: AI skills in performance reviews

3. Career paths:
   - «AI-augmented» version of every role (e.g., AI-augmented PM, AI-augmented designer)
   - New roles: AI ops, AI product, prompt engineer
   - Senior path for AI builders

4. Retention:
   - AI projects = career capital (assignment to AI work seen as opportunity)
   - Internal mobility: skill-based moves to AI-heavy teams
   - External brand: conference talks, blog posts, GitHub

5. Culture:
   - «AI-curious» as core value
   - Failed AI experiments celebrated (learning culture)
   - Cross-team AI showcases

Metric: AI skills inventory (% of workforce with documented AI proficiency).
en-talent-strategy.mistakes: Hiring ML engineers and thinking talent strategy is done. They build, but do not replace product, marketing, support skill needs. AI talent strategy = broad upskilling + targeted hiring. Not one or the other.

uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.title: Enterprise AI Transformation Roadmap
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.what: Full path from «doing AI pilots ad-hoc» to «AI-native company-wide operations». Cross-layer + cross-direction path: enterprise strategy → tactical roll-outs → org-wide change. 6-12 months of work.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.why: This is the highest-level UC in 105 Atlas — for CEO/CIO/Head of AI. Shows how a company systematically does AI transformation across ALL departments at once with governance + measurement.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.when: When the company commits to AI transformation strategically (not isolated pilots). When there is executive buy-in. When there is resource commitment ($M+ budget) for 12-24 months.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.impact: Outcome: company at Stage 3 AI-native operations in 12 months. Metrics: 4+ tactical directions running, $X ROI documented, governance in place, 80%+ team AI-proficient.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.example:
Roadmap (12 months):

Q1 (Foundation):
1. Enterprise: en-transformation-strategy → write strategy doc
2. Enterprise: en-coe → form CoE team (3-5 people)
3. Enterprise: en-governance → governance framework
4. Select first 2 tactical pilots: ai-native-customer-support OR ai-native-operations

Q2 (Tactical Pilots):
5. Launch tactical pilot #1 (highest ROI: usually Support tier-1)
6. Launch tactical pilot #2 (most strategic: usually Product or Marketing)
7. Enterprise: en-change-management → start change program
8. Enterprise: en-talent-strategy → AI upskilling roll-out

Q3 (Scale):
9. Add tactical direction #3 (based on Q2 learnings)
10. Enterprise: en-roi-measurement → measure first 6 months impact
11. Enterprise: en-risk-management → formal risk register
12. CoE → share best practices org-wide

Q4 (Maturity):
13. Add tactical direction #4 (full 4 directions running)
14. Strategy refresh based on learnings
15. Annual report to board: ROI, capabilities, risks

Stage transition: Stage 1→3 in 12 months (realistic).
Stage 4 — next 12-18 months.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.mistakes: Launching all 4 tactical directions in parallel in Q1. That is a recipe for chaos and burnout. Sequential: 1 in Q1, 2 in Q2, 3 in Q3, 4 in Q4. Each previous teaches the organization. Do not try «AI everything overnight».

uc-ai-rag-launch.title: Launch a RAG System
uc-ai-rag-launch.what: Full path from «AI does not know our documents» to «working RAG system with citations». Technical cross-layer UC through 6 nodes: [[node:ai-fundamentals|AI Fundamentals]] → Systems → Configuration. Applicable in any Transformation direction.
uc-ai-rag-launch.why: RAG is the most common production AI pattern. Each of the 5 Transformation directions (Operations/Marketing/Support/Product/Enterprise) uses RAG. This UC = technical foundation for most AI projects.
uc-ai-rag-launch.when: When AI must work with specific knowledge (documents, KB, historical data). When the LLM «does not know our facts». When you need factual grounding with citations.
uc-ai-rag-launch.impact: Outcome: working RAG pipeline in 2-3 weeks. Metrics: answer accuracy 30% (no RAG) → 85%+ (proper RAG), citation rate 100%, latency <500ms per query.
uc-ai-rag-launch.example:
Path (6 steps):

1. Foundation: af-rag-basics → understand what RAG is and its components
2. Foundation: af-embeddings → choose embedding model
3. Foundation: af-vector-db → choose vector DB (pgvector / Pinecone / Weaviate)
4. Systems: sys-rag-architecture → choose pattern (Advanced RAG minimum)
5. Foundation: projects → setup workspace + document indexing
6. Systems: sys-context-passing → properly pass retrieved context to LLM

Week 1: Decide stack + document structure.
Week 1-2: Index pilot data. Test retrieval quality.
Week 2-3: Build full pipeline. Add re-ranking. Measure.

Applicable directions: ALL (Operations reporting, Marketing content, Support knowledge, Product docs, Enterprise compliance).
uc-ai-rag-launch.mistakes: Doing Naive RAG in production. Naive (query → vector → top-K → LLM) = 50-60% accuracy. Production requires: re-ranking, hybrid search (keyword + semantic), chunk overlap, metadata filtering. Otherwise users see «AI says wrong things».

uc-ai-pilot-to-production.title: Moving an AI Pilot to Production
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.what: Path from «pilot works» to «AI in production with governance + monitoring». Cross-layer UC: Systems quality + Enterprise governance/risk + Foundation safety. Solves the most common stall point of AI projects.
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.why: The most common place where AI projects die: «pilot worked, but scale-up stuck». Reasons: no quality gates, no governance, no risk awareness. This UC provides a structured transition.
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.when: When there is a successful AI pilot (>1 month of operation). When there is a decision «production roll-out». When customer data, real money, or brand-facing outputs are involved.
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.impact: Outcome: production-ready AI system in 4-6 weeks. Metrics: 0 high-severity incidents in first 90 days, governance compliance documented, quality monitoring established.
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.example:
Path (7 steps):

1. Foundation: b-safety → review safety considerations for production
2. Systems: sys-quality-gates → add formal quality gates to the workflow
3. Systems: sys-workflows-basics → document workflow architecture
4. Foundation: prompting → freeze + version all prompts
5. Enterprise: en-governance → governance review (data classification, vendor, DPA)
6. Enterprise: en-risk-management → identify AI-specific risks + mitigations
7. Transformation: relevant quality-monitoring node (cs-quality-monitoring as pattern)

Week 1: Audit the pilot. Identify gaps.
Week 2-3: Add quality gates + monitoring. Document everything.
Week 4: Governance review + approval.
Week 5-6: Gradual roll-out with monitoring. Iterate.

Stage transition: 1→2 for the specific use case.
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.mistakes: Skipping the governance review. «The pilot worked!» — but production has accountability, audit, compliance the pilot did not have. Without review = incident waiting to happen. Governance takes 1-2 weeks, saves months.

uc-ai-roi-estimation.title: Estimating AI Project ROI
uc-ai-roi-estimation.what: Framework for estimating ROI before launch and measuring after. Cross-layer UC: Enterprise ROI + analytics from all 4 tactical directions + Foundation data. Answers the executive question: «show me the money».
uc-ai-roi-estimation.why: AI projects often do not get budget because of «unclear ROI». This UC provides a structured approach: baseline → projection → measurement → iteration. Turns «AI will help» into «AI will deliver $X over Y months».
uc-ai-roi-estimation.when: Before a budget request for an AI initiative. Quarterly review of existing AI projects. After 3-6 months of AI in production (real ROI measurement). When prioritizing AI vs other investments.
uc-ai-roi-estimation.impact: Outcome: documented ROI framework + first measurement in 4 weeks. Metrics: budget approval rate, accuracy of projections (real vs projected ROI), quarterly ROI tracking.
uc-ai-roi-estimation.example:
Path (6 steps):

1. Enterprise: en-roi-measurement → core framework (cost vs value vs attribution)
2. Foundation: sc-data → how to gather baseline data
3. Foundation: sc-analysis → analysis approach
4. Transformation: relevant analytics node (ops-reporting-automation for Operations or mk-performance-analytics for Marketing)
5. Foundation: prompting → AI-assisted ROI calculations (for consistency)
6. Cross-domain: link with other analytics (cs-support-analytics, pd-product-analytics for the full picture)

Week 1: Define cost categories + value categories for the specific initiative.
Week 2: Collect baseline data (60-90 days history if possible).
Week 3: Build ROI projection (best/expected/worst case).
Week 4: Setup measurement pipeline. Document assumptions.

Quarterly: actual vs projected. Refine the model.
uc-ai-roi-estimation.mistakes: Counting only direct cost savings. AI brings: time savings + quality improvement + capability gains + risk reduction + future optionality. Holistic ROI = real picture. Without all 5 categories — ROI looks low, initiative cancelled prematurely.

uc-ai-vendor-selection.title: AI Vendor and Stack Selection
uc-ai-vendor-selection.what: A structured approach to choosing AI tools: LLM provider, vector DB, monitoring, integration tools. Cross-layer UC: Enterprise governance/risk + Foundation pl-compare. Solves «which Claude/GPT/Open Source?».
uc-ai-vendor-selection.why: Bad vendor decisions = months of lost time + lock-in. Good decision-making = explicit criteria + structured evaluation. This UC gives the framework.
uc-ai-vendor-selection.when: Before a major AI initiative (>$50k investment). Annual technology review. When the existing vendor becomes unreliable. When scaling beyond a single team.
uc-ai-vendor-selection.impact: Outcome: documented vendor selection with reasoning in 2-3 weeks. Metrics: decision quality (look back in 6 months — was it the right call?), reduced vendor churn.
uc-ai-vendor-selection.example:
Path (6 steps):

1. Foundation: af-llm-basics → understand LLM model differences (size, architecture, training data)
2. Foundation: pl-compare → [[node:pl-web-setup|Claude.ai]] vs Code vs API vs others
3. Foundation: pl-api → API economics (cost per million tokens, rate limits)
4. Enterprise: en-governance → governance requirements (DPA, data residency, audit)
5. Enterprise: en-risk-management → vendor lock risk, fallback strategy
6. Foundation: m-security → security review checklist

Process:
  Week 1: Define use case + requirements. List criteria with weights.
  Week 2: Shortlist 3-5 vendors. Test pilots with each.
  Week 3: Score, negotiate, decide.

Framework criteria:
- Quality (model capability on our task)
- Cost (per-token + projected total monthly)
- Latency (p50/p99)
- Security (DPA, encryption, audit logs)
- Vendor stability (funding, traction, longevity)
- Lock-in (data portability, API abstractability)
- Support (responsive, technical depth)
uc-ai-vendor-selection.mistakes: Deciding based on a single benchmark. Benchmarks are biased and measure generic capabilities. Test on YOUR specific tasks. If 5 vendors → take 10 representative tasks → blind test → score. That is the real-world signal.

uc-ai-multi-agent-system.title: Multi-Agent System Orchestration
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.what: Path to building a multi-agent system: multiple specialized agents, coordination, context passing, error recovery. Advanced cross-layer UC for technical teams.
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.why: Single-agent systems work up to a certain complexity. Beyond that: you need decomposition + specialization + coordination. Multi-agent — this is next-level architecture for AI workflows.
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.when: When a single-agent system has reached its complexity limit. When the task has clear subtasks with different expertise. When parallelism is needed in AI processing. Advanced usage (after 6+ months of experience).
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.impact: Outcome: working multi-agent system in 4-6 weeks. Metrics: task completion rate, latency vs single-agent, cost per completed workflow, debuggability score.
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.example:
Path (6 steps):

1. Foundation: agents → understand agent fundamentals
2. Foundation: ag-principles → agent design principles
3. Foundation: cc-subagents → implement subagents in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] (if applicable)
4. Foundation: ag-managed → Claude Managed Agents if using Claude
5. Systems: sys-workflows-basics → workflow patterns for coordination
6. Systems: sys-context-passing → critical for multi-agent: how context flows

Architecture patterns:
  - Coordinator-Worker: one main agent delegates sub-agents specific tasks
  - Debate: 2-3 agents argue, coordinator decides
  - Reflection: agent + critic agent + revision agent
  - Tool-using agent: agent + multiple tools (search, calc, code-exec)

Week 1-2: Decompose the problem. Design agent roles.
Week 3-4: Build agents individually. Test in isolation.
Week 5-6: Compose with orchestration. Iterate on coordination failures.

Key: structured logging + replay debugging.
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.mistakes: Jumping into multi-agent from nothing. If a single-agent feels limited — first improve prompts + tools + RAG. Multi-agent adds complexity quadratically: debugging, monitoring, cost, latency. Use ONLY when single-agent provably maxed out.

ai-orchestration.title: A team of multiple AIs
ai-orchestration.what:
Sometimes one AI isn't enough. The task is too big, requires different skills, needs steps that depend on each other. Then you build an AI team: one writes, another checks, a third decides what to do next.

Like a real team: each AI has its own role, they hand work over to each other, and you watch from the outside.
ai-orchestration.why:
One AI in a complex task is like asking a single person to be a copywriter, editor, fact-checker and lawyer at the same time. They can do all of it — but poorly.

A team of AIs lets each one focus on its piece. Output quality jumps not because the model is smarter, but because each role is set up properly.
ai-orchestration.when:
When you notice:
- One AI handles a task at 70% quality — there's a ceiling
- The task has clear stages with different skills (research → writing → fact-check → polish)
- You want repeatable quality without retrying 5 times
- A single prompt has turned into a wall of text with 20 rules — impossible to maintain (for base patterns see [[node:sys-multi-agent-patterns|Multi-Agent — 4 ways]])
ai-orchestration.impact:
One AI: 70% acceptable outputs.

Team of AIs: 90% acceptable outputs. Not because the model improved, but because each step has clear focus.

Main point: instead of fighting one prompt that does it all, you assemble a team where each member does one thing well.
ai-orchestration.example:
Writing analytical articles:
1. **Researcher AI**: takes the topic, finds 10 sources, makes a summary with facts and quotes
2. **Outline AI**: takes the research, builds an article structure (intro, 3 blocks, conclusion)
3. **Writer AI**: takes the outline, writes the first draft in the brand voice
4. **Fact-checker AI**: takes the draft, checks every claim against sources, marks doubtful ones
5. **Editor AI**: removes water, tightens long sentences
6. Person: reads, makes final edits, publishes

Result: 1 hour of work instead of a day. Each step is debuggable separately.
ai-orchestration.mistakes:
Main mistake: build a team of AIs for a simple task. If one AI handles it well — don't complicate.

Second mistake: not setting clear interfaces between AIs. "AI 1 gives some text, AI 2 figures out what to do with it" = chaos. Each step needs a clear input and output format.

Third mistake: not adding humans in the right places. A fully autonomous team of AIs without checkpoints will drift in unexpected directions in 2 weeks.

ai-human-collaboration.title: AI + Human — who does what
ai-human-collaboration.what:
The border between "AI does it itself" and "calls a human". Worried AI will send something dumb to a client? Or the opposite — that every action will require your approval and you'll sit there as an operator?

AI-Human Collaboration is about where to draw that line: what AI does itself, what it shows you for review, what it doesn't touch at all.
ai-human-collaboration.why:
Without an explicit line, AI is either too cautious (calls a human for everything — annoying) or too autonomous (sent something weird to a client — embarrassing).

The right line: AI does 70% of tasks itself, 25% shows a draft to a human, 5% doesn't touch at all.
ai-human-collaboration.when:
When you're wondering:
- Can we trust AI to send client emails without review?
- What if AI gets a financial report wrong?
- Where's the line between "assistant" and "autopilot"?
- The team is afraid to give AI more permissions, but reviewing everything manually doesn't scale
ai-human-collaboration.impact:
A well-tuned border: AI works fast and autonomously where it's safe, humans step in where it matters.

Wrong: either "AI sent rubbish to a client — shut it down" or "AI asks for approval 200 times a day — turned off because it's annoying".

Main point: people work on hard things, AI works on the repetitive ones.
ai-human-collaboration.example:
Customer support at a SaaS startup:
- AI answers "how to change password", "where to download an invoice", "when does my plan renew" on its own — 70% of tickets
- AI drafts a reply and shows a human for "bug complaint", "refund question" — 25%
- AI doesn't touch "legal claims", "major accounts", "security" — 5% goes straight to a senior (mechanics — see [[node:sys-escalation-paths|Escalation: when AI calls a human]])

Result: a team of 3 handles what used to need 8.
ai-human-collaboration.mistakes:
Main mistake: "let AI write drafts for now, we'll review everything". A week later the team is burned out reviewing identical drafts and starts sending without looking. Better: explicitly say "these 5 ticket types AI handles itself, these 3 — for review".

Second mistake: setting a threshold by AI confidence ("if confidence > 80% — send"). AI is always confident. Set the border by task type, not by "model confidence".

ai-operations.title: AI in production — so it doesn't break in a month
ai-operations.what:
You shipped an AI feature → it works → 2 weeks later quality drops → users complain → you don't know why. AI Operations is a set of practices to prevent that.

It includes: watching what AI actually replies (instead of trusting "it's fine"), measuring quality regularly, controlling how much you spend on the API, versioning prompts like code.
ai-operations.why:
AI doesn't behave like regular software. Regular code: wrote it → works → works. AI code: wrote it → works → a month later the model is updated → behaves differently.

Without AI Ops your AI = an eternal pilot. With AI Ops — a production system that lives for years.
ai-operations.when:
From day one in production. Not "when we need to" — by then it's too late.

Signals you're missing Ops:
- You don't know how much you spent on AI last month
- Users complain about quality — you can't verify if it actually got worse
- The prompt was changed 5 times — you don't remember which version is in prod
- AI started answering oddly — you don't know if the model was updated or the prompt was edited
ai-operations.impact:
Without Ops: an AI feature lives 3 months, then "something broke", the team gets tired of fixing it → they kill it.

With Ops: an AI feature lives 2+ years, you spot degradation in a day instead of a month, costs are predictable.

Main point: you run the system, not the other way around.
ai-operations.example:
AI support chat in a B2B SaaS:
1. Every week 50 typical questions are auto-run (see [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|How to actually check AI works]]) → answer quality checked → if it drops 10%, alert
2. A daily Slack report: "yesterday 340 requests, $4.20 spent, 92% positive feedback"
3. All prompts live in git, costs under control (see [[node:sys-cost-management|How not to go broke on the AI API]]), changes need review from 2 people
4. If AI starts answering 30% longer than usual → automatic alert (often a sign of degradation)

The team catches issues in a day, not a customer complaint two weeks later.
ai-operations.mistakes:
Main mistake: "we'll launch first, think about monitoring later". A month in you have 10,000 requests and zero data about what AI said. You can't even tell if quality got worse.

Second mistake: measuring only "works / doesn't work". You need to measure quality — otherwise you'll miss slow degradation where AI answers technically correctly but not what's needed.

ai-integration-systems.title: AI inside the tools you already use
ai-integration-systems.what:
AI in Slack, where you already chat. AI in Notion, where your docs live. AI in Linear, where the tickets are. Integration means AI comes to your tools, not the other way around.

The opposite: "open ChatGPT → copy context → paste → copy the answer → paste back". Nobody keeps doing that for long.
ai-integration-systems.why:
AI without integration = a cool demo that nobody uses. Because switching between Slack and ChatGPT and back is exhausting.

AI inside the tool that's already open = used every day, no reminders needed.
ai-integration-systems.when:
When you notice:
- You shipped an AI tool → the team is impressed → 2 weeks later nobody opens it
- People say "cool, but I forget it exists"
- Most of the team's work lives in Slack / Notion / Linear / CRM
- AI = a separate tab people close first
ai-integration-systems.impact:
AI in chat: 10-20% of the team uses it.
AI inside Slack/Notion: 60-80% use it.

Not because it works better — because there's no need to go anywhere.

Main point: AI becomes part of the workflow, not a separate step.
ai-integration-systems.example:
A sales team works in HubSpot (under the hood — [[node:sys-api-patterns|API integration patterns]]). Before:
1. Rep sees an email from a customer
2. Goes to ChatGPT
3. Copies the conversation history
4. Asks "write a follow-up"
5. Copies the result back to HubSpot

Now:
1. Rep sees the email in HubSpot
2. Clicks "AI follow-up" right in the card
3. AI already knows the customer's history, recent deals, tone of voice
4. Gets 3 draft options
5. Picks one → tweaks → sends

From 5 minutes to 30 seconds. But more importantly — the rep actually does it, instead of "forgetting about AI".
ai-integration-systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: build a "portal" — a separate website where all AI features live. Nobody goes there. Better to embed AI into 1 tool the team uses daily.

Second mistake: integrate AI everywhere at once. You'll get 10 half-baked integrations. Better 1 integration that actually works (Slack or Notion or CRM — pick one).

sys-multi-agent-patterns.title: Multi-Agent — 4 ways AIs work as a team
sys-multi-agent-patterns.what:
Multi-Agent isn't "throw a few AIs at the task and hope". There are 4 standard ways they work together:

1. **Coordinator-Worker** — boss + executors. Boss splits the task, executors do their part, boss assembles the result.
2. **Debate** — two AIs argue about an answer, a third decides who's right.
3. **Reflection** — one AI does the work, another reviews and gives feedback, the first revises.
4. **Tool-using** — one AI but it can call functions: search the web, run code, query a database.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.why:
Knowing the patterns saves time. Without them you'd reinvent the wheel for every project. With them you say "let's use Reflection here" — the team knows what that means, builds it in a day.

It's like in cooking: knowing "sauté", "simmer", "poach" — you don't explain step by step every time, you just name the technique.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.when:
**Coordinator-Worker** — when the task can be split into independent pieces (e.g. "research 5 competitors" = 5 workers in parallel).

**Debate** — when the answer is non-obvious and you want to check different angles (legal questions, strategic decisions).

**Reflection** — when quality matters and the first try is usually "meh" (writing texts, generating code).

**Tool-using** — when AI needs real data (current weather, database, [[node:cap-search|web search]]). Most common pattern in production.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.impact:
The right pattern = your AI system works predictably, costs are clear, you can debug it.

The wrong pattern = expensive, slow, can't tell why something broke. Like baking a cake on a frying pan: technically possible, in practice — pain.

Main point: pick a known pattern, don't invent your own.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.example:
Customer support tier-1 → tier-2 escalation = Coordinator-Worker pattern:

1. Coordinator AI gets the message, classifies the type (password / billing / bug / complaint)
2. Routes to a specialized worker: password → Worker A (has password reset instructions), billing → Worker B (sees the customer's billing), bug → Worker C (knows current known issues), complaint → human
3. Worker does their part, returns the answer
4. Coordinator wraps it in a nice format and sends to the customer

Result: 4 specialized AIs handle 80% of tickets. Each is simple. You can debug if classification breaks — by looking at the coordinator, not the whole system.
sys-multi-agent-patterns.mistakes:
Main mistake: "let's use all 4 patterns at once". You'll get a system no one understands, including you. Start with one — usually Tool-using or Coordinator-Worker.

Second mistake: Reflection without limits. "AI writes, another AI reviews, the first rewrites, the second reviews again..." — they can loop for hours. Always cap the iterations (max 2-3 rounds).

Third mistake: Debate for simple tasks. Two AIs arguing about "capital of France" = waste of money. Debate only for genuinely non-obvious questions.

sys-escalation-paths.title: When AI calls a human — and how to do it right
sys-escalation-paths.what:
Escalation is the moment AI says "a human is needed here" (big picture — [[node:ai-human-collaboration|AI + Human]]) and hands off. Sounds simple, but the details matter: when it escalates, what it prepares for the human, what happens after.

Bad escalation: "AI couldn't do it, you figure it out". Good escalation: "AI couldn't do this specific thing, I've already gathered context, tried these options, recommend looking here".
sys-escalation-paths.why:
Without escalation, AI either keeps trying the same failing approach (annoying the customer), or gives up on the first hurdle (then why have it at all).

Good escalation = AI does 70% of the work, hands off the hard 30% pre-warmed. The human opens the task and immediately gets it.
sys-escalation-paths.when:
Set explicit escalation rules:
- Customer wrote "complaint" / "cancellation" / "lawsuit"
- AI failed twice in a row
- Deal amount above a threshold
- Task category marked "always human"
- Customer explicitly said "get me a human"
sys-escalation-paths.impact:
Without rules: AI either tortures the customer with endless attempts, or calls a human for every little thing.

With rules: 80% of tasks AI handles itself, 20% go to a human with ready context. Human spends not "an hour figuring it out" but "5 minutes to make a call".

Trust in the system goes up for everyone: customers, agents, management.
sys-escalation-paths.example:
E-commerce support:
1. Customer: "my order didn't arrive"
2. AI checks tracking → stuck at sorting center → writes "order is delayed, expected delivery on such-and-such date"
3. Customer: "this is the third time, I want a full refund"
4. AI detects "refund" + "third time" → escalation
5. AI prepares for the agent: "customer Ivanov, order #1234, 3rd delay in 2 months, previously ordered $50k, status — angry. Recommendation: refund + promo code. Conversation history: link"
6. Agent opens → sees full context → makes a decision in 2 minutes

Customer: gets a live person quickly. Agent: doesn't spend 20 minutes on "tell me again".
sys-escalation-paths.mistakes:
Main mistake: escalate by AI confidence ("if confidence < 80% — call a human"). AI is almost always confident. Either it doesn't escalate at all, or escalates randomly.

Better: escalate by task type and keywords — that's explainable.

Second mistake: passing a "bare" task to the human without context. The agent spends time figuring out what AI already knew. Always prep a summary before handoff.

sys-evals-benchmarks.title: How to actually check that AI works well
sys-evals-benchmarks.what:
Evals aren't "tested on 5 examples and seems ok". It's a set of 50-200 typical tasks you regularly run AI against: quality, accuracy, style.

When you change the prompt or model — you run them and see if it got better or worse. Without guessing.
sys-evals-benchmarks.why:
Without evals you don't know if AI actually works. Might work. Might seem to work. Might work on your examples and break on real users.

With evals you have a number: "80% of answers are good". Changed the prompt — became 85%. Progress is visible.
sys-evals-benchmarks.when:
When AI is out with users. Not "when we need it" — by then it's too late. (Part of [[node:ai-operations|AI Operations]] — production-readiness practices.)

Signals you're missing evals:
- You want to improve a prompt, but don't know if changes helped
- Users complain about quality — you can't tell if it really got worse
- Thinking of switching models — no data to compare
- The team argues "AI works" / "no it doesn't" — no numbers
sys-evals-benchmarks.impact:
Without evals: the team tweaks prompts "by feel". Half of changes make it worse, nobody notices.

With evals: every change is backed by a number. You see what works and what doesn't. Quality grows steadily, not "got lucky sometimes".

Main point: you manage quality instead of praying.
sys-evals-benchmarks.example:
AI assistant for writing B2B sales emails:
1. Collected 100 examples: topic + brief context + expected style
2. Each example has a "gold standard" answer (written by a human or manually validated)
3. Each prompt change is run on these 100 → AI scores similarity to the gold + a human spot-checks
4. You see: "previous version — 72% good answers, new — 81%". Ship the new one.
5. Weekly automatic run → if it drops below 75% (model degradation) → alert

The team sees real progress, not "feels a bit better".
sys-evals-benchmarks.mistakes:
Main mistake: "we'll do evals later". A year in, you have 1,000 users and zero data on quality. When something breaks — you can't tell if it really broke.

Better: 30 examples from day one. Expand as you grow.

Second mistake: scoring only "correct / incorrect". AI quality is a spectrum: accuracy, style, length, tone. You need to measure several attributes separately.

sys-cost-management.title: How not to go broke on the AI API
sys-cost-management.what:
AI calls cost money. At launch — pennies. As you scale — can hit tens of thousands a month if you don't watch.

Cost Management is a set of simple practices: use the cheap model where you can, cache repeats, monitor spend daily. Not "optimization for its own sake" but "don't pay extra".
sys-cost-management.why:
AI spend grows silently. Today $50, in 3 months $5,000, another 3 — $30,000. Nobody notices because they're thinking "$0.001 per request — nothing".

If you monitor — you manage. If you don't — one day you get a bill and a shock.
sys-cost-management.when:
From day one in production (one of the core [[node:ai-operations|AI Operations]] practices). Not "when money becomes a problem" — by then the habit of overspending is set.

Signals you need cost management urgently:
- Don't know how much you spent last month
- Using the most expensive model "just in case"
- Not caching repeating requests
- Same AI calls in different parts of the product with different prompts
sys-cost-management.impact:
Without management: you overpay 3-5×. Part goes to "AI answers the same questions over and over", part to "using Opus where Haiku would do".

With management: spend is predictable, easy to plan. Often you can cut the bill 2-3× without losing quality.

Main point: you can run AI at scale without fearing the bill.
sys-cost-management.example:
SaaS chat support, 10,000 requests per day:

Before: all requests go through Sonnet, $0.015 per request → $4,500/month.

After:
1. AI first classifies the question type with cheap Haiku ($0.001)
2. Simple questions ("where's my invoice", "how to change password") → Haiku ($0.001)
3. Complex ("integration not working") → Sonnet ($0.015)
4. Very complex (~5%) → Opus with detailed analysis
5. FAQ answers cached → 30% of requests don't hit AI at all

Result: $1,200/month. Same or better quality (Opus where Sonnet used to struggle).
sys-cost-management.mistakes:
Main mistake: use the most powerful model "just in case". Opus costs 15× more than Haiku. On 80% of tasks the quality difference is invisible.

Better: cheap model by default, expensive only where really needed.

Second mistake: not caching repeating requests. If 30% of users ask the same FAQ — serve from cache, don't pay AI again.

sys-api-patterns.title: How AI talks to other systems
sys-api-patterns.what:
When AI needs to interact with your software (big topic — [[node:ai-integration-systems|AI Integration Systems]]) (CRM, email, database) — it goes through an API. There are 4 standard ways: reply immediately, kick off and report later, react to events, stream the answer piece by piece.

Picking the way = answering "how long does AI take" and "do we need the answer right now".
sys-api-patterns.why:
Wrong choice = AI is working, but the user sits staring at a spinner. Or the opposite: the user needs an instant answer, and you built a queue.

The right pattern = the user sees what they expect: "fast" when it's fast, "working on it" when it's slow.
sys-api-patterns.when:
**Reply immediately (sync)** — AI handles it in 1-3 seconds (short texts, classification, simple answers).

**Kick off and report (async)** — AI runs 30+ seconds (document analysis, big report generation). User starts → goes for coffee → gets a notification.

**By event (webhook)** — external trigger: email arrived / customer submitted a form / a task appeared.

**Piece by piece (streaming)** — long answer, user sees AI typing (like ChatGPT).
sys-api-patterns.impact:
Right pattern = UX doesn't annoy. The user either gets an answer instantly, or understands AI is working in the background, or sees progress.

Wrong = "clicked a button → waited 30 seconds staring at the screen". Half the users close the tab.

Main point: technology is tuned to user expectations, not the other way around.
sys-api-patterns.example:
AI assistant in a SaaS product:

1. **Sync**: "classify the task type" — 1 second, sync, button returns the answer immediately
2. **Async**: "full quarterly analysis" — 2 minutes, user kicks it off → keeps working → gets "report ready" notification
3. **Webhook**: a customer wrote in Intercom → external webhook triggers AI → AI drafts a reply in the agent's inbox
4. **Streaming**: "write a long email" — AI types piece by piece, user sees it being written, can interrupt if it's going off track

Each case — its own pattern. Don't try to do everything through one.
sys-api-patterns.mistakes:
Main mistake: do everything sync. User clicks a button → waits 40 seconds → nothing happens → closes the tab → AI finishes anyway → money spent, result is useless.

Better: if AI runs longer than 5 seconds — async with notification.

Second mistake: streaming where it's not needed. If the answer is short and arrives fast — streaming just complicates the code for no value.

ai-native-design.title: AI for design teams
