ai-native-design.what:
Design = "do 5 interviews → synthesize → sketch 10 prototypes → gather feedback → redo". Many steps, each slow.

AI speeds up everything between "the research is done" and "the final mockup": synthesizes interviews, generates prototype ideas, checks accessibility, supports the design system, writes UX copy.
ai-native-design.why:
A designer spends 60% of time on "prep work": organizing research, routine edits, consistency checks. AI removes the routine — the designer focuses on creativity and strategy.

Main point: AI doesn't "draw for you". It speeds up everything around drawing so you have more time to think.
ai-native-design.when:
When you notice:
- 10 user interviews sit in Notion, you synthesized two
- Every week you check by hand that mockups have alt text
- A design system exists but everyone draws their own way
- UX copy is written by the product writer, you wait 2 days
- "Prototype variants" eat 3 days, you end up picking the first one
ai-native-design.impact:
Before: synthesizing 10 interviews = a week.

After: AI does the first-pass synthesis in 2 hours, designer verifies and finalizes → 1-2 days.

Before: 3 prototype variants in a day — not enough time.

After: AI generates 10 idea variants in an hour, designer picks 3 and goes deep.

Main point: more time on "deciding what's better", less on "gathering material".
ai-native-design.example:
7 directions inside:
- [[node:ds-design-research|Research synthesis — working with interviews]]
- [[node:ds-prototype-generation|Prototype idea generation]]
- [[node:ds-design-ops|Design ops automation]]
- [[node:ds-accessibility|Accessibility audits]]
- [[node:ds-design-system|Design system evolution]]
- [[node:ds-content-design|Content / UX copy]]
- [[node:ds-team-workflow|Team workflows]]
ai-native-design.mistakes:
Main mistake: expecting AI to "come up with the design for you". It won't. AI gives variants — your job is to pick and refine.

Second mistake: using AI for final mockups. AI is good at sketches and drafts. On final mockups your hand and taste decide.

Third mistake: automating design review. "AI will check the design for consistency" — won't replace design review with the team. Use AI for mechanical checks (alt text, contrast), but design judgement — on humans.

ds-design-research.title: AI Design Research
ds-design-research.what: AI-powered user research for designers: synthesis of usability tests, behavioral analysis of session recordings, competitor design pattern analysis. From «100 interviews = 2 weeks of processing» — to «AI extracts themes in an hour, designer validates».
ds-design-research.why: Research is a critical part of design, but time-intensive. The designer spends 50% of time on synthesis, 50% on actual design. AI shifts the balance to 20/80.
ds-design-research.when: Usability testing rounds (5-15 sessions). Competitor research. Card sorting analysis. When there are session recordings and you need to extract patterns.
ds-design-research.impact: Time-to-insight: days → hours. Theme extraction structured instead of «designer's gut feel».
ds-design-research.example:
Usability Synthesis Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - 10 session recordings (transcripts)
  - User interview notes
  - Pre/post task survey data
        ↓
  AI Steps:
  1. Extract pain points (frequency + severity)
  2. Group by user task / journey stage
  3. Identify quick wins vs structural issues
  4. Generate improvement hypotheses
        ↓
  Designer validates:
  - Pain point severity rated through design lens
  - Solutions ranked by feasibility
        ↓
  Output: structured research report + prioritized backlog

Metric: time-to-insight, design improvements shipped.
ds-design-research.mistakes: Doing AI synthesis without designer eye-on-data. AI misses emotional nuance, frustration patterns, edge cases. Workflow: AI extracts themes → designer reviews 20% with original recordings → confidence in the rest.

ds-prototype-generation.title: AI Prototype Generation
ds-prototype-generation.what: AI generation of prototypes: design mockup → HTML/React code, sketches → Figma compositions, multiple style variants in minutes. From «designer codes prototype for 2 days» — to «AI provides 5 variants in an hour, designer selects + refines».
ds-prototype-generation.why: Prototyping is a bottleneck in the design cycle. AI handles the «technical» aspect (turn idea into code/Figma), the designer focuses on concept + critique.
ds-prototype-generation.when: Early-stage exploration (need many variants quickly). Design system component variants. Conversion of mockup to code. A/B testing variant generation.
ds-prototype-generation.impact: Time-to-prototype: 2 days → 4 hours. Variant coverage: 1-2 → 5-10 per concept. Iteration speed: 2-3× faster.
ds-prototype-generation.example:
Prototype Workflow:

  Designer brief:
  «Onboarding flow for B2B SaaS,
   3 steps, brand color #2563eb,
   font Inter, mood: friendly+confident»
        ↓
  AI Step 1: Generate 5 layout variants
        ↓
  Designer selects 2 most promising
        ↓
  AI Step 2: Generate React/HTML for each
        ↓
  Designer refines via Figma OR direct code edits
        ↓
  Output: working prototype 4 hours after brief

Real usage: AI-generated code = starting point, not final. Designer refines 30-50%.
ds-prototype-generation.mistakes: Expecting «pixel-perfect output» from AI. AI gives 70% from idea to code, the last 30% (taste, brand fit, accessibility) — designer. Treating AI as starting point = speed. Treating as final = mediocre output.

ds-design-ops.title: AI Design Operations
ds-design-ops.what: Automating design ops: asset documentation, component change-logs, Figma library management, design QA. From «we have everything but no one knows where» — to «AI maintains documentation continuously».
ds-design-ops.why: Design ops are invisible until they break. Asset chaos, outdated components, missing docs — all kill velocity. AI maintains this continuously without manual effort.
ds-design-ops.when: Design system exists but is poorly documented. Multiple designers, components diverge. New hires ask «where is X component?». Pre-handoff QA is not performed.
ds-design-ops.impact: Designer time on ops: -50%. New hire onboarding: 2 weeks → 1 week. Component reuse: +30% (instead of reinvention).
ds-design-ops.example:
Design Ops Automation:

1. Component Documentation:
   - AI reads Figma file → generates MD docs per component
   - Updates: AI diffs changes weekly → adds changelog

2. Asset Audit:
   - AI scans products → finds inconsistent components
   - Flags: «button styles diverge across 5 screens»

3. Handoff QA:
   - Pre-handoff AI checks: token usage, accessibility, spacing
   - Generates QA report for dev review

4. Library Health:
   - Weekly: AI identifies unused components, outdated tokens
   - Suggests cleanup

Metric: design system health score, time saved on documentation.
ds-design-ops.mistakes: Doing AI design ops without integration into actual tools. «AI generates docs in a separate Notion» = no one reads. AI must live where designers work: Figma plugins, Slack integrations, CI/CD for design.

ds-accessibility.title: AI Accessibility Automation
ds-accessibility.what: AI a11y checks at every step: contrast checks, alt-text generation, screen reader simulation, keyboard navigation audit. From «accessibility = a special audit once every six months» — to «accessibility-by-default through AI».
ds-accessibility.why: Accessibility is often checked at the end, when fixing is expensive. AI catches issues in real-time during design. Cost is 10× lower.
ds-accessibility.when: Design system accessibility setup. New feature launches with user-facing UI. Quarterly product audits. Customer complaints about a11y issues.
ds-accessibility.impact: A11y bug rate: 30% → 5% (issues caught at design stage). Compliance: WCAG AA reached confidently. Legal risk: significantly reduced.
ds-accessibility.example:
A11y Automation Pipeline:

  Design phase:
  1. AI checks contrast ratios on every screen
  2. Auto-generates alt-text suggestions for images
  3. Flags missing focus states, keyboard traps
  4. Reviews color usage (color as sole indicator?)

  Pre-handoff:
  5. Full WCAG checklist auto-run
  6. Report: issues + recommendations + WCAG criteria mapping

  Post-launch:
  7. Real screen reader test simulation
  8. AI describes UX as a blind user would experience it

Metric: WCAG compliance %, a11y issues per release.
ds-accessibility.mistakes: Thinking AI = «full a11y replacement». Manual testing with real assistive tech (real screen readers, real keyboard navigation) — still required. AI catches 80%, the last 20% — manual + user testing with a11y users.

ds-design-system.title: AI Design System Evolution
ds-design-system.what: AI helps evolve the design system: token set generation, component variants, documentation for every component, usage migration on breaking changes. Design system from a «static document» to «a living system with an AI helper».
ds-design-system.why: Design systems usually stagnate: no resources for maintenance, breaking changes are postponed. AI removes the operational burden — the system stays fresh.
ds-design-system.when: Design system exists but maintenance burden is high. Migration to a new token system. Component variants need to be created (sizes, states, themes). Documentation is scattered across different places.
ds-design-system.impact: Design system update velocity: 3-5× faster. Migration speed: weeks → days. Documentation freshness: always current.
ds-design-system.example:
Design System Evolution:

1. Token Generation:
   - Designer says «brand uses warm palette, modern feel»
   - AI generates: color scale, spacing scale, typography scale
   - Designer refines: 70% AI output → 30% manual adjustment

2. Component Variants:
   - Designer creates base button
   - AI generates: sizes (sm/md/lg), states (default/hover/focus/disabled), themes (light/dark)
   - Outputs Figma file + code stubs

3. Breaking Change Migration:
   - «We changed token spacing from 4px to 8px»
   - AI scans codebase + Figma files
   - Generates migration PR + Figma changes list

4. Documentation:
   - AI maintains MDX docs per component
   - Updates on component changes automatically

Metric: components shipped, time-to-update.
ds-design-system.mistakes: Relying entirely on AI for design system decisions. The design system embodies brand strategy + UX principles — these are critical human decisions. AI = executor, not decision-maker for system architecture.

ds-content-design.title: AI Content Design
ds-content-design.what: AI help with UX writing: microcopy for buttons/forms/errors, onboarding flows, empty states, helper text. From «designer writes copy in free time» — to «AI generates contextual copy, designer curates voice».
ds-content-design.why: UX copy is critical for UX, but designer time on copy is always insufficient. AI generates options, the designer chooses + refines by brand voice.
ds-content-design.when: New feature launches with substantial UI text. Onboarding flow design. Error message standardization. International product (multiple languages).
ds-content-design.impact: Copy generation time: -70%. Coverage: 100% of UI elements have intentional copy (vs «TBD»). Consistency: brand voice maintained across the product.
ds-content-design.example:
Content Design Workflow:

For each UI surface:
  1. Designer provides context: «password reset flow, friendly tone»
  2. AI generates 5 variants for each microcopy slot:
     - Page title
     - Description (1 sentence)
     - Primary CTA
     - Error states (3-5 likely errors)
     - Success state
  3. Designer picks the best + may refine
  4. AI suggests improvements based on brand voice
  5. Final copy documented in content style guide

For i18n:
  - AI does first-pass translation
  - Local copywriter refines (we still need humans here)

Metric: copy coverage %, brand voice consistency score.
ds-content-design.mistakes: Using AI for legal/compliance copy without review. «AI wrote it» does not release from accountability. Critical copy (privacy notices, ToS, regulatory text) — human-written, AI only for review.

ds-team-workflow.title: AI Design Team Workflow
ds-team-workflow.what: Design team operating model with AI: shared Figma plugins, design system AI helpers, weekly «AI office hours» for designers, AI-aware critique sessions. From «every designer with their own Claude» — to a «design-augmented team».
ds-team-workflow.why: Individual designer AI usage does not scale — voice is inconsistent, components diverge, lessons are not learned. Team workflow consolidates AI value.
ds-team-workflow.when: Design team ≥3 designers actively use AI. When the product is design-driven (consumer apps, brand-heavy). When inconsistent AI usage causes brand fragmentation.
ds-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: +25-35%. Brand consistency: significantly improved. Designer career growth: «AI-augmented designer» as senior path.
ds-team-workflow.example:
Design Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project «Design Workspace»:
   - Brand voice guide indexed
   - Design system docs accessible
   - Past research synthesized
   - Component library reference

2. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]: design principles, brand voice, accessibility rules.

3. Skills (Figma plugins + Claude):
   - microcopy-generator
   - component-doc-writer
   - accessibility-checker
   - research-synthesizer

4. Weekly rituals:
   - «AI office hours» (30 min): designers share wins/failures
   - Quarterly «AI in design» retrospective

5. Critique enhancements:
   - Pre-critique: AI runs accessibility/brand checks
   - Critique focuses on craft + concept (not finding bugs)

Stage 3 sign: new designer productive in 3-5 days.
ds-team-workflow.mistakes: Making «AI in design» = «designer is required to use AI». Forced adoption kills creative ownership. AI must be «discovered through value» — designers choose to use it when it makes them better, faster, happier.

uc-ai-design-research-launch.title: Launch AI Design Research
uc-ai-design-research-launch.what: Full path from «we have a mountain of research material and no time to process it» to «AI-powered research pipeline for the design team». Cross-layer path through 6 nodes.
uc-ai-design-research-launch.why: The most common design team request: «we have tons of user research, but we cannot process it. Designers spend time on synthesis, not on actual design». This UC solves it systematically.
uc-ai-design-research-launch.when: When there are ≥10 session recordings or interview transcripts. When design ops is unbalanced (lots of research input, little synthesis output). When there is buy-in from Head of Design.
uc-ai-design-research-launch.impact: Outcome: working research pipeline in 2 weeks. Metrics: time-to-insight 2 weeks→2 hours per round, research coverage 30%→100%, structured theme library.
uc-ai-design-research-launch.example:
Path (6 steps):

Week 1: Foundation setup.
1. Foundation: prompting → how to formulate synthesis prompts for research
2. Foundation: af-rag-basics → research repository indexing
3. Foundation: projects → create a «Design Research» Project with files

Week 1-2: Workflow build.
4. Systems: sys-context-passing → passing research context between stages
5. Transformation: ds-design-research → concrete synthesis workflow

Week 2: Team adoption.
6. Transformation: pd-discovery-research → cross-link with PM workflow for shared insights

Day 1-3: Index existing research (sessions, transcripts).
Day 4-7: Test synthesis on 5 sessions. Designer validates → refine prompts.
Day 8-14: Full pipeline + team training + first real research round.

Stage transition: 1→2.
uc-ai-design-research-launch.mistakes: Doing a UC without designer-PM alignment. Design research and Product research are separate in most companies. If the synthesis pipeline is only for designers, PMs duplicate the work. Sync with pd-discovery-research = synergy, not duplication.

ai-native-ecommerce.title: AI for eCommerce
ai-native-ecommerce.what:
Flagship transformation direction: how AI changes how catalog, merchandising, CRO, support, and analytics teams work in an online store. 15 nodes with explicit workflows, metrics, and links to Foundation/Systems.

This isn't "AI recommendations" in the abstract — it's concrete scenarios: "10k SKUs with no descriptions → AI generates PDPs in minutes", "site search returns nothing → semantic search via embeddings", "CRO tests take 6 weeks → AI generates variants in an hour".
ai-native-ecommerce.why:
E-commerce is the clearest vertical market for AI: processes are documented, metrics are measurable, ROI is measurable directly (revenue, conversion, AOV). This makes the domain the best ground for systematic AI adoption.

The key: AI here isn't cosmetic — it replaces existing manual processes. PDP copywriters, merchandisers, analysts — all get 5-10× leverage from AI at the same headcount.
ai-native-ecommerce.when: When the catalog has >500 SKUs and the content team is ≤5. When conversion has plateaued for 3-6 months. When search returns "no results" >20% of the time. When merchandising is manual and goes stale within a day. When the service team is drowning in routine queries. When entering a new market and localization is needed.
ai-native-ecommerce.impact:
Across the whole direction the expected shifts: PDP time-to-publish 4h → 5min, search conversion +20-40%, average recommendation quality +30%, support load −50% on tier-1, time-to-insight on data days → hours.

Key point — measurability: every rollout can be counted in revenue within 90 days.
ai-native-ecommerce.example:
15 nodes in the direction, grouped by value stream:

**Catalog:** [[node:ec-pdp-gen|AI PDP Generation]], [[node:ec-search-opt|AI Search]], [[node:ec-merchandising|AI Merchandising]], [[node:ec-recommendations|AI Recommendations]]

**Conversion:** [[node:ec-cro|AI CRO]], [[node:ec-experimentation|AI Experimentation]], [[node:ec-checkout-opt|AI Checkout Optimization]], [[node:ec-personalization|AI Personalization]]

**Operations:** [[node:ec-support|AI Commerce Support]], [[node:ec-loyalty|AI Loyalty]], [[node:ec-analytics|AI Analytics]], [[node:ec-pricing|AI Pricing]], [[node:ec-inventory|AI Inventory]], [[node:ec-segmentation|AI Segmentation]]

**Team:** [[node:ec-team-workflow|Team Workflow]]
ai-native-ecommerce.mistakes:
The main mistake — trying "everything at once". 15 nodes = a map of possibilities, not an adoption roadmap. Start with one node, give it 60-90 days, count ROI, then expand.

Second mistake: AI generation with no quality gate. On a 10k SKU catalog a badly tuned AI will produce 10k bad cards in an hour — worse than 100 good manual ones. A quality gate is mandatory.

Third: not localizing brand voice. Generic AI-English on a Finnish or Russian market is spotted by shoppers instantly.

ec-pdp-gen.title: AI PDP Generation
ec-pdp-gen.what:
Automated generation of Product Detail Pages from raw data: AI creates SEO title, meta description, marketing body, and attribute tables from product specs, images, and a brand voice guide.

Input: CSV with name, attributes, photos. Output: CMS-ready card in 3 languages.
ec-pdp-gen.why: Catalog teams can't keep up with new products. 10k SKUs = 10k hours of manual copywriting. AI covers 80% of that work in 2-3 minutes per SKU at comparable quality — freeing copywriters for strategic work (brand guides, longreads, CRO copy).
ec-pdp-gen.when: Catalog >500 SKUs and content team ≤5. Localization needed in 3+ languages. SEO metrics worse than competitors. Regular new assortment (>50 SKUs/month).
ec-pdp-gen.impact: Time-to-publish: 4 hours → 5 minutes per SKU. Coverage (% of cards with full copy): 30% → 100%. SEO traffic: +25-40% over 3 months on new cards. Localization cost: −70%.
ec-pdp-gen.example:
Workflow:

[CSV: name, attributes, image_url, category]
  ↓
[Step 1: extract product type + key attributes]
  ↓
[Step 2: SEO title (60 chars) + meta (160 chars)]
  ↓
[Step 3: marketing body (300-500 words) in brand voice]
  ↓
[Step 4: attribute table HTML]
  ↓
[Quality gate: human review OR auto-publish if score > 0.85]
  ↓
[Output: CMS draft]

Real example: 500 SKUs → 500 drafts overnight. Editor validates 50 random ones → tunes brand voice prompt → next batch ships without edits.
ec-pdp-gen.mistakes:
Launching on the whole catalog at once — quality degrades on the long tail. Start with 50-100 SKUs + brand voice tuning.

No quality gate — the catalog gets cluttered with generic text that readers spot.

No voice localization — generic UK English in the Finnish market puts buyers off.

ec-search-opt.title: AI Search Optimization
ec-search-opt.what:
Semantic search on embeddings: the user types "warm jacket for winter" → AI finds "down jacket" even if the title contains neither "warm" nor "winter".

Hybrid approach: keyword (exact matches) + semantic (by meaning) + reranking (Claude picks the best).
ec-search-opt.why:
Classic keyword search loses 20-40% of queries: synonyms, typos, the buyer's wording doesn't match the product name. Every "no results" is lost conversion.

Semantic search closes the gap, but needs embeddings, a vector DB, and reranking — Claude is particularly strong at the final stage.
ec-search-opt.when: On the site >20% of search sessions end in "no results". Long queries (>3 words) show low CTR. Catalog >5k SKUs across diverse categories. Multilingual site.
ec-search-opt.impact: Search conversion: +20-40%. "No results" rate: 25% → 5%. Average time to click on a result: −30%. Bounce rate on the search result page: −15%.
ec-search-opt.example:
Architecture:

[User query: "jacket for minus 20"]
  ↓
[Step 1: Embedding query → vector]
  ↓
[Step 2: Vector search in the product index → top-50 candidates]
  ↓
[Step 3: Keyword filter (category, price, availability)]
  ↓
[Step 4: Claude rerank: for each candidate — how well does it match the query? Returns top-10 with reasoning]
  ↓
[UI: products + explanation "why these"]

Real: companies adding semantic search see +25% conversion from search traffic within 60 days.
ec-search-opt.mistakes:
Replacing keyword search entirely — you lose exact matches on SKUs and brand names. Hybrid only.

Indexing only the title — you skip attributes, descriptions, reviews. Embeddings should be built from the full product context.

Ignoring stale data. The vector DB must be re-indexed when the catalog changes, otherwise search shows out-of-stock products.

ec-personalization.title: AI Personalization
ec-personalization.what:
Adapting UX to the individual shopper: home page, recommendations, copy change based on browsing history, purchases, and segment.

Claude here isn't a recommender system (that's a separate node) — it's a layer that interprets behaviour and makes personalization decisions.
ec-personalization.why:
Generic UX gives generic conversion. Personalization adds 30-50% to e-commerce metrics — a long-known fact, but implementation used to be expensive (data team, ML engineers, MLOps).

AI lowers the entry cost: a single Claude agent with access to profile + behaviour can decide "show X or Y" without dedicated ML infrastructure.
ec-personalization.when: Catalog >1k SKUs and >10k active shoppers. Sharply different segments (B2C and B2B on one site, or distinct price tiers). Visible retention gap between segments (meaning the experience doesn't fit some of them).
ec-personalization.impact: Conversion for returning users: +30-50%. AOV: +10-25%. 30-day retention: +15-30%. CTR on home page recommendations: +40-60%.
ec-personalization.example:
Architecture:

[User session start]
  ↓
[Load user context: profile + last 10 views + last 3 purchases + segment]
  ↓
[Claude: "Which categories/collections are relevant? What tone of copy fits?"]
  ↓
[Output: { hero_collection, recommended_categories[5], voice_attributes[3] }]
  ↓
[Render homepage with these parameters]

Real: a SaaS-eCommerce raises retention by 22% within a quarter of basic personalization rollout.
ec-personalization.mistakes:
Personalizing everything. First personalize 1-2 high-value surfaces (home, search results). If it works — expand.

Ignoring cold start. For a new buyer there is no data — you need a fallback to segment or generic. Do not show "hi, we don't know you".

Not measuring. Personalization without an A/B test = faith, not science. Compare with a control group.

ec-merchandising.title: AI Merchandising
ec-merchandising.what:
AI curator for collections: "summer collections for women 25-35" are assembled automatically from catalog + sales + trends, not by a merchandiser by hand.

Claude reads sales data + catalog metadata + seasonal signals → suggests 10-20 collections with rationale.
ec-merchandising.why:
Merchandising is a bottleneck in most stores: 1-2 merchandisers per 10k SKUs. Collections go stale, new products fail to make it into collections for weeks. AI takes care of the routine "collect 20 products on a theme", a human validates.

Side effect: collections refresh daily instead of monthly — sales react to trends faster.
ec-merchandising.when: Catalog >2k SKUs. Merchandising team ≤3. Visibly stale collections on the site (older than 2 weeks). Seasonal goods — every season needs a manual refresh.
ec-merchandising.impact: Time-to-collection: 4 hours → 20 minutes. Active collections: 15 → 50+ simultaneously. Sales from curated collections: +30-50%. Reaction time to trends: weeks → days.
ec-merchandising.example:
Workflow:

[Trigger: weekly merchandising review]
  ↓
[Input: catalog snapshot + last 30 days of sales + trending searches]
  ↓
[Claude: "Which 10 collections will be relevant next week? For each — name, description, 15-25 products, rationale"]
  ↓
[Human review: merchandiser validates in 10 minutes]
  ↓
[Publish to CMS]

Real: instead of 5 collections refreshed monthly — 30 collections refreshed weekly.
ec-merchandising.mistakes:
Auto-publish without a human gate — AI may assemble a collection from out-of-stock or low-margin products.

Ignoring business rules (minimum margin, exclusion rules). Without them AI optimizes "by relevance" and the business loses money.

Forgetting the baseline. Compare AI collections to manually curated ones to see the real uplift.

ec-cro.title: AI Conversion Rate Optimization
ec-cro.what:
Claude as conversion analyst: generates hypotheses from data, proposes A/B variants of copy and UI, and after the test explains why a variant won or lost.

Does not replace the CRO specialist, but speeds up ideation and synthesis 5-10×.
ec-cro.why:
The main CRO bottleneck isn't running tests — it's hypothesis generation and result analysis. One hypothesis takes an hour of discussion, a post-mortem takes a day of analysis.

Claude does both phases in minutes, leaving humans with validation and strategic decisions.
ec-cro.when: Site with >10k visitors/month (statistical significance is feasible). A CRO function exists or at least 1 specialist. Conversion has plateaued for 3+ months. The team needs ideas, not tools.
ec-cro.impact: Hypothesis throughput: 2-3 per week → 10-15. Time-to-postmortem: 2 days → 2 hours. Cumulative conversion uplift over a quarter: +15-25% (driven by more fast iterations).
ec-cro.example:
Workflow:

[Input: current funnel data + competitors + reviews]
  ↓
[Claude: "5 hypotheses for improving product page conversion with rationale"]
  ↓
[CRO picks 1-2, formulates the test]
  ↓
[Claude: "3 CTA copy variants + 3 hero-image briefs"]
  ↓
[Run A/B test for 2 weeks]
  ↓
[Claude: "Result analysis: variant B won on conversion, lost on AOV. Likely cause — X. What to test next — Y"]

Real: teams move from 1 test per month to 1 test per week at the same headcount.
ec-cro.mistakes:
Testing AI-generated variants without human review — they may contain factual errors about the product.

Testing everything. AI generates plenty of ideas, but a valid CRO test = 1 variable over 2 weeks. Prioritization discipline = a more useful workflow than speed.

Replacing the CRO specialist. AI = acceleration, not a replacement for a domain expert.

ec-experimentation.title: AI Experimentation
ec-experimentation.what:
A systematic approach to experiments: AI generates a hypothesis backlog, helps in test design, monitors running tests, spots early signals, and analyses results.

Integrates with existing A/B tools (Optimizely, VWO, GrowthBook), does not replace them.
ec-experimentation.why:
Without AI, experimentation stalls at two points: ideation (where do hypotheses come from) and synthesis (what does the result mean). Between them the test itself uses tools you already have.

AI closes both ends — hypothesis flow grows, the learning loop gets denser.
ec-experimentation.when: The team already runs ≥4 tests per month. A data analyst exists (or you want to unblock through AI). Experimentation has become routine with no strategy — many tests, little learning.
ec-experimentation.impact: Tests per quarter: +50-100% at the same headcount. Learning velocity: every test produces a structured insight rather than "variant B kinda seems better". A knowledge base of past tests accumulates automatically.
ec-experimentation.example:
Quarterly experimentation review:

[Input: 30 tests run last quarter + results]
  ↓
[Claude: "Which insights recur? Which hypothesis categories drove uplift? Where did we burn cycles?"]
  ↓
[Output: structured retrospective + proposed experimentation roadmap for next quarter]

Real: teams on this approach move from "we test whatever comes to mind" to "we test by an impact × confidence priority matrix".
ec-experimentation.mistakes:
Trusting AI early signals. A test must reach stat-sig — AI may "see" a confident pattern on a 50% sample and tempt you to stop early.

Not documenting. AI is only useful if it has history. Without a structured archive of past tests every new test starts from scratch.

Forgetting confidence intervals. AI can give a narrow answer to a broad question — always look at uncertainty.

ec-checkout-opt.title: AI Checkout Optimization
ec-checkout-opt.what:
AI reads funnel data → finds drop-off points → proposes hypotheses for why → generates variants for testing.

Checkout specifics: every step is critical, expensive to redesign. AI helps prioritize what to change.
ec-checkout-opt.why: Checkout is the most expensive part of the funnel to optimize (you risk breaking payments). Most teams fear touching it. AI lowers the risk through data-driven prioritization: you only change where drop-off is largest and the hypothesis is strongest.
ec-checkout-opt.when: Checkout completion rate <70%. Mobile checkout visibly worse than desktop. Multi-step checkout (>3 pages). Regular support complaints about "I can't pay".
ec-checkout-opt.impact: Checkout completion: +5-15 percentage points. Mobile gap (desktop − mobile): narrows by 50%. Time-to-find-friction: days → hours.
ec-checkout-opt.example:
Monthly checkout review:

[Input: GA4 funnel data + heatmaps + support tickets about checkout]
  ↓
[Claude: "Top-3 friction points, each with evidence: where people drop, what they ask support, what microcopy may be the cause"]
  ↓
[Output: prioritized backlog with estimated impact]
  ↓
[Engineering takes the top-1 item, tests it, revisits it after 30 days]

Real: teams find and fix 3-5 mid-impact friction points per quarter instead of the usual "maybe we rewrite checkout once a year".
ec-checkout-opt.mistakes:
Changing many steps at once — impossible to attribute impact. Only one change per test.

Ignoring payment failures. AI reads GA4 but does not see payment provider errors. That data has to be brought in separately.

No segmentation. Mobile/desktop, new/returning, paid/organic visitors behave very differently. AI without segmentation gives an averaged (and therefore useless) picture.

ec-recommendations.title: AI Recommendation Systems
ec-recommendations.what:
Personal recommendations on embeddings + history: "you might like", "bought together", "next purchase".

Claude is used at two points: reranking (pick the best from a top-50 candidate set) and explanation ("why this is recommended to you").
ec-recommendations.why:
Recommendations are one of the highest-ROI AI cases in e-commerce: 20-35% of all revenue at large stores comes through recommendations. But classic approaches (collaborative filtering, market-basket analysis) require a data scientist and infrastructure.

Generative AI lowers the bar: embeddings + Claude reranking give 80% of the quality of classic systems at 20% of the complexity.
ec-recommendations.when: Catalog >1k SKUs. Active users >5k/month. Repeat purchase rate >10% (there is data for personalization). Currently no recommendations in place — so there's a clear baseline for measurable uplift.
ec-recommendations.impact: Revenue from recommendations: 0 → 15-25% of total. AOV: +10-20%. Cross-sell rate: +30-50%. CTR on recommendations: 3-8% (vs 0.5-1.5% on random).
ec-recommendations.example:
Architecture:

[User views product X]
  ↓
[Embedding similarity: top-50 similar products]
  ↓
[User history filter: remove what was already bought/viewed]
  ↓
[Claude rerank: "from these 50, which 6 are most relevant for this user specifically? Account for history + price + availability"]
  ↓
[Render: 6 products + explanation for each ("you viewed similar items in category Y")]

Real: companies adding explainability to recommendations see +15% CTR vs unexplained.
ec-recommendations.mistakes:
Only collaborative filtering on small data — runs into a "cold start" problem.

Not filtering out-of-stock and low-margin — AI optimizes for clicks, the business loses money.

Not measuring against random. Without an A/B baseline you don't know how much better AI is than "random recommendations".

ec-support.title: AI Commerce Support
ec-support.what:
Claude as a tier-1 support agent for e-commerce: answers routine questions (order status, returns, shipping), escalates the hard cases to a human.

Integration with order management + knowledge base + escalation rules. A concrete application of [[node:cs-tier1-automation|tier-1 automation]] in the commerce domain.
ec-support.why:
In e-commerce 70-80% of support queries are routine: "where is my order", "how do I return", "when will it arrive". It's a workload on agents that delivers no value (no upsell, no relationship).

AI closes those 70-80% instantly, agents only work on hard cases (disputed returns, B2B specifics, payment issues).
ec-support.when: Support team drowning in routine queries. Response time >2 hours on simple questions. >20% of queries are about order status. CSAT drops due to slow responses.
ec-support.impact: Tier-1 deflection rate: 60-80%. Response time on simple questions: 2 hours → instant. Agent capacity on complex cases: +200%. CSAT: +0.3-0.7 points.
ec-support.example:
Architecture:

[Customer query: "where is my order #12345"]
  ↓
[Claude: identifies intent = order_status]
  ↓
[Tool call: GET /orders/12345]
  ↓
[Response: "Your order shipped on May 23, expected delivery May 25, tracking number X"]

[Customer query: "I want to return an item, it's broken"]
  ↓
[Claude: identifies intent = return_with_defect → escalation rule "defect = human"]
  ↓
[Escalate to agent with context: order details + customer history + photo upload prompt]

Real: an e-commerce store cuts tier-1 ticket volume by 65% in 60 days.
ec-support.mistakes:
Auto-escalating everything — no deflection, support team is not unloaded. Define clear escalation rules upfront.

Not syncing the knowledge base. AI answers from old return policies → the real policy changed → complaints.

Ignoring tone. Generic AI tone in support drives people away. Brand voice tuning is mandatory.

ec-loyalty.title: AI Loyalty Systems
ec-loyalty.what:
Personal loyalty programs: AI analyses behaviour → identifies a segment → picks relevant offers (cashback %, exclusive products, early access).

Not "one program for everyone" — an adaptive one tied to the customer lifecycle.
ec-loyalty.why:
Generic loyalty programs (buy 10 times = 10% off) give flat results. AI-driven loyalty matches offers to individual motivation: VIPs get exclusive access, churning customers get win-back offers, new ones get an onboarding bonus.

ROI rises at the same program spend.
ec-loyalty.when: Active buyer base >5k. Repeat purchase rate >15% (there is something to grow). Current loyalty program at <5% redemption (means it isn't working). Team ready for segmented messaging.
ec-loyalty.impact: Loyalty program engagement: 5% → 30-40%. Repeat purchase rate: +15-25%. CLV (customer lifetime value): +20-35%. Churn rate: −10-20%.
ec-loyalty.example:
Quarterly loyalty review:

[Input: all customers + behaviour data + program history]
  ↓
[Claude: "Segment the base into 5 groups: VIP, Active, Cooling, At-Risk, Churned. For each — what offer is optimal with rationale"]
  ↓
[Output: program structure + messaging + estimated impact]
  ↓
[Marketing/Loyalty team validates, launches]
  ↓
[After 30 days: Claude analyses results, refines segmentation]

Real: moving from a flat 10% loyalty to segmented loyalty gives +25% retention in 90 days.
ec-loyalty.mistakes:
Ignoring unit economics. Generous offers for VIPs can eat the margin. AI must respect business constraints.

Not measuring. Without A/B segments vs control group you can't prove uplift.

Forgetting exit. AI is great at finding churn signals — use it for save campaigns too, not only for acquisition.

ec-analytics.title: AI Commerce Analytics
ec-analytics.what:
Claude as commerce analyst: reads GA4 + sales data + ad spend → writes insights with hypotheses and action items.

Replaces "here's a dashboard, figure it out" with "here's what happened this week and what to do".
ec-analytics.why:
Most e-commerce teams drown in data without actionable insights. An analyst is needed but expensive and slow. AI gives the first-pass analysis, the analyst validates and digs deeper.

Decision velocity grows: instead of a weekly review with a 3-5 day delay, you get daily insights by morning.
ec-analytics.when: Sales >$100k/month. The team looks at metrics weekly but the action item rate is low. No dedicated analyst, or there is one but 80% of their time goes to reports, not analysis. Anomalies in data are spotted late.
ec-analytics.impact: Time-to-insight: 3-5 days → 1 day. Anomaly detection lag: weeks → 24 hours. Quality of weekly reviews: structured insights vs "here are the numbers".
ec-analytics.example:
Daily commerce briefing:

[Input: yesterday's GA4 + sales + ads spend + inventory]
  ↓
[Claude: "Daily summary: revenue ±X% vs avg, top movers by category, anomalies, hypotheses for each, 3 action items for today"]
  ↓
[Slack post in #commerce-daily at 9:00]
  ↓
[Team comments, refines, executes]

Real: teams move from monthly "what happened" to daily "what we are doing" — a sharp rise in ownership at the team level.
ec-analytics.mistakes:
Using AI as an attribution engine. AI does not know the real multi-touch attribution model. Use it for narrative, not for exact causation.

Ignoring data quality. AI will produce confident insights on broken data. Check GA4 + sales reconciliation before automating.

Not documenting. AI is good when it has history — without an archive of past insights every day starts from scratch.

ec-pricing.title: AI Pricing Optimization
ec-pricing.what:
AI helps with pricing decisions: analyses demand signals, competitor prices, cost structure, margin targets → recommends optimal prices and promotional triggers.

Not automatic pricing (risk of catastrophic mistakes), but decision support for the merchandiser / pricing manager.
ec-pricing.why:
Pricing is a high-ROI lever: a 1% pricing improvement yields 8-12% to profit for a typical e-commerce business. But classical pricing tools are expensive and need a data science team.

Claude + structured data can cover 60-70% of that value at 20% of the cost — especially for teams without a dedicated pricing analyst.
ec-pricing.when: Catalog >500 SKUs. Margin varies >20% across categories. Competitors >5 in the main categories. Pricing decisions are manual and rare (a few times a year).
ec-pricing.impact: Gross margin: +1-3 percentage points. Pricing review frequency: quarterly → weekly. Time-to-promotion-decision: days → hours.
ec-pricing.example:
Weekly pricing review:

[Input: SKU-level sales last 30 days + competitor prices (scraped) + inventory levels + margin targets]
  ↓
[Claude: "10 SKUs where price elasticity suggests a price hike is possible. 5 SKUs where competitors are 15%+ lower — recommend match or differentiate. 3 SKUs with inventory build-up — promotion needed with estimated impact"]
  ↓
[Pricing manager validates, updates the system]

Real: teams find and use 3-5 pricing opportunities a month instead of the usual 1-2 a quarter.
ec-pricing.mistakes:
Auto-applying pricing changes. AI may miss a supplier contract (minimum price) or promo commitments. Human in the loop is mandatory.

Ignoring elasticity differences. AI may recommend +5% on an elastic product — you lose more in volume than you gain in margin.

Not validating competitor data. Scraping breaks. AI on bad data produces bad recommendations.

ec-inventory.title: AI Inventory Intelligence
ec-inventory.what:
AI helps with inventory decisions: demand forecasting, replenishment triggers, slow-mover detection, recommendations on dead stock clearance.

Combines historical sales + seasonality + current signals (search queries, traffic to categories).
ec-inventory.why:
Inventory management has two risks: overstock (cash trapped, eventual writedown) and stockout (lost revenue + customer satisfaction). Classical forecasting tools are heavy and need integration.

AI offers a middle ground: structured analysis on existing data without heavy infrastructure.
ec-inventory.when: Catalog >1k SKUs. Regular stockouts on bestsellers OR dead stock buildup. Manual inventory review is rare (monthly or less). Forecast accuracy is low (>30% error on quarterly forecast).
ec-inventory.impact: Stockout rate on bestsellers: −50-70%. Dead stock: −30-50%. Inventory turn ratio: +20-40%. Cash tied in inventory: −15-25%.
ec-inventory.example:
Weekly inventory briefing:

[Input: SKU sales velocity + current stock levels + lead times + seasonal patterns]
  ↓
[Claude: "Top-20 SKUs where stockout is likely in the next 14 days — restock needed. Top-10 slow movers >90 days — recommend clearance promo with estimated lift. Seasonal signals — spring is coming, raise inventory in category X"]
  ↓
[Buying team validates, places PO]

Real: teams on this approach cut stockouts on bestsellers by 60% in a quarter.
ec-inventory.mistakes:
Trusting the forecast without human override. AI is good at pattern detection, bad at unprecedented events (viral post, competitor shutdown).

Ignoring supplier constraints. AI optimizes for demand, but lead times and MOQ are real constraints.

Not measuring forecast accuracy. Without a feedback loop AI does not improve. Every month — review where AI was wrong and why.

ec-segmentation.title: AI Customer Segmentation
ec-segmentation.what:
AI discovers natural segments in the customer base: not "men 25-35" (demography), but behavioural ("buy every 2 weeks, discount-sensitive, open email in the evening").

Used as input for personalization, loyalty, marketing campaigns.
ec-segmentation.why:
Demographic segmentation is outdated — real behaviour rarely depends on gender/age. Behavioural segmentation used to need a data scientist + clustering algorithms.

Claude + embeddings can find 5-8 meaningful behavioural segments in an hour of work, instead of a month-long ML project.
ec-segmentation.when: Active customers >5k (data needed for signals). Generic marketing — everyone gets the same emails. Conversion rate varies sharply between cohorts without an understanding of why.
ec-segmentation.impact: Email engagement: +50-100% (segmented vs blast). Campaign ROI: +30-60%. Marketing budget efficiency: same revenue at −20-30% spend.
ec-segmentation.example:
Quarterly segmentation refresh:

[Input: all-customer feature vector — frequency, recency, AOV, categories, channel preferences, time-of-day patterns]
  ↓
[Embedding clustering: 6-8 natural groups]
  ↓
[Claude: "For each group — characteristics, size, value, recommended engagement strategy"]
  ↓
[Output: segment definitions + targeting recipes for marketing / loyalty / CRM]

Real: moving from RFM segmentation to behavioural gives +40% engagement at the same email volume.
ec-segmentation.mistakes:
Creating too many segments. >10 segments = the team can't operationalize them. Sweet spot: 4-8 actionable groups.

Not refreshing. Customer behaviour shifts. Quarterly refresh at minimum.

Ignoring business meaningfulness. The algorithm may find a cluster, but if you can't explain "who they are and what to offer them" — it is noise, not signal.

ec-team-workflow.title: Commerce Team AI Workflow
ec-team-workflow.what:
How an e-commerce team orchestrates AI: a shared Project with brand voice, catalog templates, weekly AI office hours, knowledge sharing across roles (merchant, content, CRO, support, analyst).

This is a meta node: it ties the previous 14 into a team workflow.
ec-team-workflow.why:
Individual AI usage in commerce does not scale — different roles use it their own way, voice drifts, insights are lost across functions. Team workflow = shared standard + shared library + cross-functional learning.

A company that puts AI workflow at the team level pulls 6-12 months ahead of those that leave it at the individual level.
ec-team-workflow.when: Commerce team ≥4 people use AI. Inconsistent results between roles appear. New team members "don't know how we work with AI". Duplication of effort across functions is visible.
ec-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: +30-50%. Onboarding time: 2 weeks → 3-5 days. Cross-functional learning: shared Project = the team sees each other's prompts and insights. Quality consistency: voice + templates + skills.
ec-team-workflow.example:
Commerce Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project "Commerce Workspace"
2. Files: brand voice guide, product taxonomy, content templates, brand do/don't
3. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]: usage rules + naming conventions
4. Reusable Skills: pdp-writer, search-rerank, weekly-briefing, customer-segment-analyzer
5. Weekly "AI office hours", 30 min: team shares wins and fails
6. Quarterly review: which AI workflows delivered ROI, which did not

Stage 3 sign: a new team member is productive in 5 days, cross-functional projects run on shared AI infrastructure.
ec-team-workflow.mistakes:
A team with no ownership. "Everyone uses AI" = nobody owns the workflow. Every part (voice, templates, skills) must have an owner.

Individual heroes. The team's most productive AI user accumulates knowledge in their head — when they leave, knowledge leaves. Shared infrastructure from day one.

Ignoring measurement. Without metrics "AI usage" = abstract. Track time saved, quality uplift, ROI on specific workflows.

uc-ai-personalization-launch.title: Launch AI Personalization in the Store
uc-ai-personalization-launch.what:
Full path from "we have generic UX for everyone" to "working personalization for returning customers". Cross-layer path through 7 nodes: Foundation → Systems → Transformation.

Real scope: 6-8 weeks, 1-2 people on the team.
uc-ai-personalization-launch.why: Personalization is the highest-ROI e-commerce case (+30-50% conversion for returning users). But teams often delay it: "we need ML infra", "we need data scientists", "expensive". This UC shows how to start without an ML team.
uc-ai-personalization-launch.when: Catalog >1k SKUs. Active returning customers >5k. Team: senior engineer + product manager + analyst. Readiness to invest 6-8 weeks.
uc-ai-personalization-launch.impact: Outcome: working personalization on home page + email + recommendations in 2 months. Metrics: returning conversion +30-50%, AOV +10-25%, retention +15-30%.
uc-ai-personalization-launch.example:
Path (7 steps):

Week 1-2: Foundation.
1. Foundation: [[node:af-embeddings|af-embeddings]] — products as vectors
2. Foundation: [[node:af-memory-systems|af-memory-systems]] — user context persistence
3. Foundation: [[node:af-vector-db|af-vector-db]] — vector storage setup

Week 3-4: Systems.
4. Systems: [[node:sys-rag-architecture|sys-rag-architecture]] — retrieval pattern for recommendations
5. Systems: [[node:sys-context-passing|sys-context-passing]] — passing user context

Week 5-6: Transformation.
6. Transformation: [[node:ec-personalization|ec-personalization]] — concrete workflow
7. Transformation: [[node:ec-recommendations|ec-recommendations]] — recommendation engine

Week 7-8: Iterate.
A/B test vs control group, refine prompts, expand surfaces.
uc-ai-personalization-launch.mistakes:
Starting with email personalization. Looks cheaper, but returning users more often come directly to the site. Start with home page recommendations — bigger impact.

No cold start. For a new user there is no data — the fallback should be generic but not "we don't know you".

Not measuring. Without A/B vs control you can't prove AI personalization is better than generic UX.

uc-ai-product-search.title: Launch Semantic Catalog Search
uc-ai-product-search.what:
Full path from "keyword search misses products" to "hybrid semantic search with reranking". 6 steps, 4-6 weeks.

Key point: don't throw away the existing keyword search — add a semantic layer on top of it.
uc-ai-product-search.why:
Search is a critical funnel point. 20-40% of conversion is lost to "no results". Every search conversion improvement translates directly into revenue.

Semantic search is the most direct ROI case for embeddings in e-commerce.
uc-ai-product-search.when: Catalog >5k SKUs. >15% of search sessions → "no results". Search bounce rate is high. Multilingual site OR many synonyms in categories.
uc-ai-product-search.impact: No-results rate: 25% → 5%. Search conversion: +20-40%. Time-to-first-click on a result: −30%.
uc-ai-product-search.example:
Path (6 steps):

Week 1: Foundation.
1. [[node:af-embeddings|af-embeddings]] — catalog as vectors
2. [[node:af-vector-db|af-vector-db]] — vector index setup

Week 2-3: Systems.
3. [[node:sys-rag-architecture|sys-rag-architecture]] — retrieval pattern
4. [[node:prompting|prompting]] — reranking prompt design

Week 4-5: Transformation.
5. [[node:ec-search-opt|ec-search-opt]] — hybrid search workflow
6. [[node:ec-recommendations|ec-recommendations]] — bridge to recommendations

Week 6: Production rollout with A/B test.
uc-ai-product-search.mistakes:
Replacing keyword search entirely. For exact SKU matches keyword wins. Hybrid is mandatory.

Not re-indexing. The catalog changes → the vector DB must update. Without a feedback loop search shows out-of-stock products.

Ignoring query analytics. AI is good at searching but does not explain why people search for "X". Analysing search queries is a separate, important task.

uc-ai-conversion-optimization.title: Launch an AI-Augmented CRO Program
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.what:
Full path from "we run 1-2 tests a month with no structure" to "a structured AI-augmented CRO program". 7 steps, 4-6 weeks of setup.

This isn't "AI does CRO" — it's "AI accelerates the CRO team 5-10×".
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.why:
CRO is a bottleneck on most teams: ideation is slow, post-mortems take days, the hypothesis backlog is never structured.

AI closes both ends (ideation and synthesis) — the testing tool in between stays the same.
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.when: Site >10k visitors/month (statistical significance is feasible). A CRO function exists (or at least 1 person doing it). Conversion plateau 3+ months. You need ideas, not tools.
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.impact: Hypothesis throughput: 2-3/week → 10-15/week. Time-to-postmortem: 2 days → 2 hours. Cumulative conversion uplift per quarter: +15-25%.
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.example:
Path (7 steps):

Week 1: Foundation.
1. [[node:prompting|prompting]] — how to formulate hypothesis prompts
2. [[node:pr-iterate|pr-iterate]] — iterative refinement technique
3. [[node:sc-analysis|sc-analysis]] — data analysis with Claude

Week 2-3: Systems.
4. [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|sys-evals-benchmarks]] — measuring AI suggestion quality
5. [[node:sys-quality-gates|sys-quality-gates]] — human review process

Week 4-5: Transformation.
6. [[node:ec-cro|ec-cro]] — concrete CRO workflow
7. [[node:ec-experimentation|ec-experimentation]] — broader experimentation system

Week 6: Run 3 pilot tests, refine workflow.
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.mistakes:
Trusting AI-generated variants without human review — factual errors about the product.

Testing everything. AI generates plenty, but a valid test = 1 variable over 2 weeks. Discipline > speed.

Replacing the CRO specialist. AI = acceleration, not a replacement. Prioritization discipline stays with the human.
